meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.
Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards are archived outside the ranking. Problems first resolved on or after 1 January 2026 can remain eligible, with dated evidence, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

shared_definitions.scope: Shared terminology for the green selection reviewed on 20 November 2026. Each card specifies its input representation, parameters and cost model.

entries.title: How to read the shared definitions
entries.text:
Write \(N=|\langle X\rangle|\) for the length in bits of an encoded instance \(X\). On a SAT card, \(n\) usually counts variables. On a graph card, \(n\) usually counts vertices. Read the local definition before substituting either quantity into a bound. A truth table on \(n\) variables, for example, occupies \(2^n\) bits before a threshold or header is added.

For a Boolean function \(f\), \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathcal B}(f)\) denotes its minimum circuit size under the named basis and cost convention. A given circuit \(C\) has size \(s=|C|\). For a language \(L\), \(L_n\) is its characteristic function on \(n\)-bit strings. De Morgan formula leaf size is \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\).

A card's local definitions specify its model, promises and exceptions. The linked entries supply shared terminology, also available in the JSON exports.

entries.title: Input encodings and size parameters
entries.text:
For a finitely encoded object \(X\), write \(\langle X\rangle\) for its binary description and \(N=|\langle X\rangle|\) for its complete bit length. Count signs, indices, delimiters, coefficients and all explicitly supplied lists. An explicit table or syntax tree is supplied in full; a circuit or oracle generating it is a different representation. The card specifies the representation and the treatment of malformed inputs or inputs outside a promise.

Unless a card states otherwise, integer data in a bit model are binary, and rational data are signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Unary input is an explicit exception, as for some security parameters. The magnitude of an integer is not its bit length. An algorithm polynomial in numerical magnitude may take exponential time in a binary description.

Polynomial-time decidability is invariant under encodings interconvertible in polynomial time with polynomial output length. This does not preserve a precise exponent, a linear or quasilinear bound, or a circuit-size threshold. For those targets, retain the specific encoding and account for conversion costs. Bounds in a structural parameter must also account for the full supplied input; they are not promises of that running time for arbitrarily padded descriptions. An oracle, streaming, query or exact-real model has its own explicitly stated input-access costs.

entries.title: Asymptotic bounds and quantifiers
entries.text:
All unspecified logarithms have base two. \(f(n)=O(g(n))\) means that some constant \(C>0\) bounds \(f(n)\le Cg(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\); \(f=o(g)\) means \(f(n)/g(n)\to0\) where the ratio is defined. A polynomial bound has a fixed exponent and coefficient. Constants may depend on parameters declared fixed by the card, but not on varying instances.

Failure of a polynomial upper bound means that every proposed polynomial is exceeded at arbitrarily large lengths. It does not automatically mean a superpolynomial lower bound at every sufficiently large length. Preserve the displayed quantifier order. Likewise, a single \(2^{o(n)}\)-time algorithm and a separate \(2^{\varepsilon n}\)-time algorithm for each \(\varepsilon>0\) are not interchangeable without further conditions.

\(\operatorname{poly}(N)\) denotes some fixed polynomial factor. In SAT bounds such as \(2^{o(n)}\operatorname{poly}(N)\), \(n\) counts variables and \(N\) counts encoding bits. The meaning of \(\widetilde O\) and the parameters inside its suppressed logarithmic factors must follow the individual card.

entries.title: Uniform computation and bit cost
entries.text:
In the bit model, a uniform deterministic algorithm is one finite Turing-machine program for all input lengths, using a fixed number of tapes and finite tape alphabets. Each transition costs one step. Input access, integer arithmetic, auxiliary computation and writing output count. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) on every input of length \(N\), for fixed \(C,k\). The program receives no length-dependent advice or oracle unless the card explicitly supplies one.

A nondeterministic machine accepts when at least one branch accepts. A nondeterministic time bound applies to every branch. A randomized time guarantee and an expected-time guarantee are distinguished in the randomization entry. Polynomial-time class comparisons are robust under the usual polynomial-overhead machine simulations; precise time bounds must retain the machine model selected by the card.

entries.title: Languages, P, NP and coNP
entries.text:
A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\). Membership is a total yes/no question, including the empty string. Its characteristic function at length \(n\) is \(L_n(x)=1\) exactly when \(x\in L\).

\(\mathrm{P}\) is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithms in the bit model. A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there are a polynomial \(p\) and one deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}:\ V(x,y)=1.\]
The verifier halts on every pair, with time polynomial in \(|x|+|y|\); it accepts no allowed witness on a no-instance. The program and bounds are fixed independently of \(x\). This is equivalent to nondeterministic polynomial time. A language belongs to \(\mathrm{coNP}\) exactly when its complement in \(\{0,1\}^*\) belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\). These are language classes; witness-output and promise problems require their own definitions.

entries.title: Decision and search reductions
entries.text:
A polynomial-time many-one (Karp) reduction from \(A\) to \(B\) is one total uniform deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) satisfying \(x\in A\iff f(x)\in B\). It writes one entire target instance. A language is NP-hard under these reductions when every NP language reduces to it, and NP-complete when it is also in NP. Other completeness notions must name their reduction type.

For search relations \(R,Q\), a polynomial-time many-one search reduction consists of two polynomial-time maps \(F,G\). The output instance must belong to the target domain for every input in the source domain. For every such input \(x\) and every valid answer \(z\) to \(Q\) on \(F(x)\), one requires \(R(x,G(x,z))\). Time is measured in \(|x|\) for \(F\) and \(|x|+|z|\) for \(G\). Correctness must hold for every accepted target answer. Domain and malformed-input conventions remain local.

A Turing reduction may instead make adaptive oracle queries. Logarithmic-space, randomized, promise-preserving and count-preserving reductions are separate notions. Do not replace one by another when normalizing wording.

entries.title: SAT, CNF-SAT, k-SAT and Circuit-SAT
entries.text:
SAT asks whether an explicitly encoded Boolean formula has a satisfying assignment. A formula is a finite tree over variables, constants 0 and 1, binary AND and OR, and unary NOT. Repeated subexpressions are written separately. A literal is a variable or its negation. A CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals. In this glossary, \(k\)-CNF means at most \(k\) literals per clause; an exactly-\(k\) convention must be stated locally. An empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false.

\(n\) counts variables, \(m\) counts clauses when applicable, and \(N\) is the full encoding length. Binary variable indices and delimiters contribute to \(N\). SAT, CNF-SAT and 3-SAT are polynomial-time interreducible, but a reduction may change the number of variables and the precise running-time bound. A card's restricted syntax, numbering and padding rules remain part of its problem.

Circuit-SAT receives a circuit DAG, which can share subcomputations. This is not a formula tree. MCSP instead receives a full truth table of length \(2^n\), together with its size threshold. A clause-incidence encoding of 3-SAT is another explicitly identified representation. Never identify these input lengths.

entries.title: Boolean circuits and minimum circuit size
entries.text:
A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input wires and one or more ordered outputs. Gate values can be reused; fan-out and depth are unrestricted unless restricted locally. Correctness is exact on the card's entire domain, or on its stated promise set. Circuits for different lengths are nonuniform unless a uniform constructor is explicitly required.

In the \(\mathrm{DM}\) convention, gates are binary AND and OR and unary NOT. All operation gates, including NOT, cost one; input wires, constant sources 0 and 1, wires and output designations are free. An output may be an input, a constant or a gate. In the \(B_2\) convention, any Boolean function of at most two input bits is a unit-cost gate, with the same free sources and wires. Write \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\) or \(\operatorname{CC}_{B_2}(f)\) for the minimum gate count. Multiple outputs share one joint budget.

The subscript \(\mathcal B\) in \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathcal B}\) records the basis and cost convention. In the \(\mathrm{DM+c}\) convention, constants are gates of cost one and the other De Morgan costs are the same. For a language, apply it to \(L_n\), not to the infinite language without specifying a length. \(s=|C|\) denotes the size of a given circuit, not a minimum. Fixed complete bounded-fan-in bases preserve polynomial size and linear-size existence up to constant factors; they do not preserve exact optimum sizes or exact MCSP thresholds.

A threshold-circuit card specifies how a majority gate treats an even tie and whether size charges wires. Each occurrence of a repeated input counts separately when wires are charged. Modular gates and unbounded fan-in also require a named basis. Use the card's cost convention when comparing exact size thresholds.

entries.title: De Morgan formulas and leaf size
entries.text:
A De Morgan formula is a rooted tree with binary AND/OR and unary NOT operations, variable leaves and optional constants. Internal computations cannot be shared. The size convention \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\) is the minimum number of variable-leaf occurrences in a formula computing \(f\) exactly. Positive and negative occurrences each count, including repeated occurrences of the same variable. Constant leaves are free. Constants have size zero and a literal has size one. Pushing negations to the leaves preserves this measure.

Formula leaf size, circuit gate count and circuit depth are distinct measures. A source may call formula size \(L(f)\) and circuit size \(S(f)\); revised cards use \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\) and \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\) while retaining original symbols in source quotations. Restricted, arithmetic or other formula models must retain their own cost conventions.

entries.title: L, NL and PSPACE
entries.text:
Space is the number of work-tape cells visited, with fixed finite alphabets; the read-only input is not charged. The classes \(\mathrm{L}\) and \(\mathrm{NL}\) use deterministic and nondeterministic machines, respectively, with \(O(\log(N+2))\) workspace. Nondeterministic acceptance is existential over branches; a polynomial clock can be imposed for NL. A halting deterministic logspace machine has only polynomially many configurations and therefore polynomial running time.

\(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) consists of languages decided by halting deterministic machines with polynomial workspace. It imposes no polynomial time bound. Read-only input, output-tape access, catalytic storage and other auxiliary memory conventions must not be changed when a card specifies a different space model.

entries.title: EXP, NEXP and their complements
entries.text:
\(\mathrm{EXP}\), also called \(\mathrm{EXPTIME}\), is deterministic time \(2^{N^{O(1)}}\), the union over fixed polynomial exponents. \(\mathrm{NEXP}\) is the corresponding nondeterministic class, with every branch time-bounded. Equivalent bounds can be written \(C2^{(N+1)^k}\) for fixed positive integers \(C,k\). \(\mathrm{coNEXP}\) consists of complements of NEXP languages. Machines are uniform and have no advice unless a suffix explicitly supplies it.

\(\mathrm{E}=\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{O(N)})\) and \(\mathrm{NE}=\mathrm{NTIME}(2^{O(N)})\) have linear exponents. They are distinct definitions from EXP and NEXP; any use of padding to relate particular containment questions must be justified locally.

entries.title: BPP, RP and randomized guarantees
entries.text:
\(\mathrm{BPP}\) consists of languages decided by one uniform randomized Turing machine in polynomial time on every input and every random tape, with error at most \(1/3\) on each individual input. Random bits are independent and unbiased. \(\mathrm{RP}\) has the same worst-case time convention, never accepts a no-instance, and accepts each yes-instance with probability at least \(1/2\). Constant error thresholds can be amplified within polynomial time.

A Las Vegas algorithm is always correct whenever it outputs and terminates with probability one; a claimed expected-time bound averages over its internal randomness for each fixed input. This differs from a worst-case bound on every random tape. A Monte Carlo guarantee permits a stated error probability. Average-case input distributions, simultaneous correctness over a sequence of queries, and adaptive adversaries are specified locally. Do not turn any of these into a blanket BPP guarantee.

entries.title: Nonuniformity, P/poly and advice
entries.text:
\(\mathrm{P/poly}\) consists of languages whose functions \(L_n\) have Boolean circuits of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\), for constants depending on the language. One circuit is chosen for each length; no computable circuit generator is required. This is equivalent to deterministic polynomial time with a polynomial-length advice string \(a_n\) depending only on the input length.

More generally, a suffix /poly supplies polynomial-length advice that is fixed before the instance is chosen. Advice need not be computable. For NEXP/poly, the nondeterministic running time is exponential in a polynomial of the original input length. The familiar equality of some advised classes does not establish the equality of their uniform versions. Any circuit uniformity condition, oracle, shared randomness or input-dependent information is a separate model choice.

entries.title: FP, #P and total NP search
entries.text:
FP denotes total functions computed by deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines, with output bits charged. A nonnegative integer output is written in binary unless stated otherwise. A #P function has the form
\[f(x)=|\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\}|,\]
where \(p\) is a polynomial and \(V\) a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Count distinct witness strings, even if several represent the same object. Padding must preserve these counts; ordinary existence-preserving NP reductions need not do so.

TFNP concerns polynomially balanced, polynomial-time decidable relations \(R(x,y)\) with at least one valid answer for every input. A polynomial-time algorithm for a search relation selects some valid answer. This relation-solving usage of FP is explicitly identified on search cards. Search, decision and exact counting are different tasks.

entries.title: Word RAM, real RAM and oracle access
entries.text:
A word RAM stores words of the bit width stated by the card, usually \(\Theta(\log(n+2))\). Each card lists its finite set of unit-cost instructions or explicitly selects the integer instructions below. The availability of multiplication, division, random words, packed input and precomputed tables is not inferred from the name alone. Multiword arithmetic is charged by its component operations. A polynomial-time equivalence with Turing machines does not justify transferring a precise exponent without overhead.

Integer instructions for cards that explicitly select them. On unsigned \(w\)-bit words, allow addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, comparison, copying, branching, and random-access reads and writes. Each costs one step. A shift by at least \(w\) gives zero. Multiword operations cost their component steps. A memory instruction accesses one word. Random bits or words, and the cost of generating them, are specified by the individual card.

A real RAM or algebraic model may charge exact operations on reals at unit cost. It is not a bit-cost algorithm on arbitrary precision rational data. Query and oracle models charge the specified accesses and may deliberately leave the oracle's internal computation uncharged. Streaming passes, online deadlines and data-structure preprocessing and queries keep their local costs.

entries.title: Arithmetic circuits and field conventions
entries.text:
An arithmetic circuit is a DAG computing a polynomial through arithmetic operations over the specified field or ring. Unless a card explicitly uses a different notion, polynomial equality means equality as formal polynomials, not agreement only on selected evaluation points. The field, permitted constants, division gates, commutativity and size measure are part of the model.

Boolean \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathcal B}\) does not stand for arithmetic circuit complexity. Arithmetic cards keep a field-qualified local notation and explicitly say whether they count input gates, operation gates, wires, or some combination. Arbitrary field constants of unit cost do not have the same meaning as finitely encoded binary constants. Changing among these conventions can preserve some asymptotic questions but requires checking the target; no global change of field, constants or uniformity is made here.

entries.title: Security parameters and negligible functions
entries.text:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\) when not locally rebound, and unary \(1^\lambda\) input is used when the card specifies it. Polynomial security bounds are in \(\lambda\), not in the bit length of a binary spelling of \(\lambda\). A nonnegative function \(\nu\) is negligible if, for every constant \(c>0\), \(\nu(\lambda)<\lambda^{-c}\) for all sufficiently large \(\lambda\).

The adversary's uniformity, advice, auxiliary input, oracle access, interaction and probability space are specified by the security experiment. A polynomial-size circuit adversary is not the same model as a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machine. Information-theoretic, statistical and computational guarantees must retain their quantifiers and error parameters.

entries.title: Graphs and structural size
entries.text:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). For a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\) are structural counts, not automatically its bit length. The card specifies whether edges are directed, loops or parallel edges are allowed, and whether labels, weights and a distinguished vertex form part of the input.

Adjacency matrices, adjacency lists and edge lists are different encodings. Binary endpoints typically cost logarithmically many bits, and binary weights contribute their full bit lengths. Query access to adjacency is another model. Graphs used as mathematical objects in an existence question need not be algorithmic inputs at all. No global simplicity, connectivity or representation assumption is imposed by a link to this entry.

entries.title: The polynomial hierarchy and TQBF
entries.text:
Set \(\Sigma_0^{\mathrm P}=\Pi_0^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm P\). For fixed \(k\ge1\), membership in \(L\in\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\) is expressed by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time predicate \(R\) and a polynomial \(p\). For each input \(x\), choose \(k\) strings of length \(p(|x|)\) under alternating quantifiers, starting with an existential quantifier. Then \(x\in L\) exactly when the resulting quantified predicate \(R(x,y_1,\ldots,y_k)\) is true. A block quantifies an entire string. \(\Pi_k^{\mathrm P}\) consists of the complements of these languages, and \(\mathrm{PH}=\bigcup_{k\ge0}\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\). The level, polynomial and predicate are fixed for the language.

TQBF is the language of true, fully quantified Boolean formulas. Every variable in the Boolean matrix is bound by the prefix, each quantifier ranges over one bit, and malformed encodings are rejected. The number of blocks in an input can grow with its length. TQBF is PSPACE-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions.

entries.title: Parameterized time and reductions
entries.text:
A parameterized instance has a finite description and a distinguished nonnegative integer \(k\). Let \(N\) be the complete encoded length. A fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) decision algorithm runs in \(f(k)(N+1)^c\) steps for a total computable \(f\) and one constant \(c\) independent of \(k\). The card fixes how the parameter is encoded. A polynomial exponent that may depend on \(k\) gives a different guarantee.

An FPT many-one reduction computes an equivalent target instance \((x',k')\) within such a time bound and guarantees \(k'\le g(k)\) for a total computable \(g\). Kernelization additionally uses polynomial preprocessing time and bounds the size of the resulting instance as a function of \(k\).

entries.title: Finite words and finite automata
entries.text:
An alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite set of symbols. The set \(\Sigma^*\) contains all finite words, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). Word length counts symbols. A complete one-way deterministic finite automaton has a finite state set \(Q\) and transition function \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\). Its extension to words starts at the given state and reads symbols from left to right. Acceptance uses an initial state and a set of final states when the task calls for a language.

A nondeterministic automaton can have several transitions. A word is accepted if it has an accepting run. Unambiguity permits at most one accepting run per word. Two-way heads, endmarkers, empty moves, and acceptance of infinite words use the conventions on the individual card.

entries.title: Approximation ratios and rounding
entries.text:
For a minimization problem with nonnegative costs, a factor \(\alpha\ge1\) bounds the cost of a feasible output by \(\alpha\,\operatorname{OPT}\). For a nonnegative maximization problem a card may use a fraction \(\rho\in[0,1]\) and require value at least \(\rho\,\operatorname{OPT}\). The inequality also specifies the guarantee when the optimum is zero. An additive error has the units of the objective.

For a randomized algorithm, read whether the inequality holds in expectation or with a specified probability on each instance. Expected cost and expected running time concern different random quantities. For a minimization relaxation with a positive lower bound, its integrality gap is the supremum of the integral-to-relaxed optimum ratio over the stated instances. An algorithmic target also counts the cost of finding a feasible solution.

entries.title: Total variation and mixing time
entries.text:
The total variation distance between probability laws \(\mu,
u\) on the same measurable space is \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,
u)=\sup_A|\mu(A)-
u(A)|\), where \(A\) ranges over measurable events. On a finite state space \(\Omega\) it equals \(	frac12\sum_{x\in\Omega}|\mu(x)-
u(x)|\).

For a discrete-time Markov chain with transition matrix \(P\) and stationary law \(\pi\), the worst-start mixing time at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is the least \(t\ge0\) with \(\max_x d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P^t(x,\cdot),\pi)\le\varepsilon\), or infinity if there is no such time. A transition, a whole sweep and one unit of continuous time have different costs. The card fixes the clock, starting law and tolerance.

entries.title: Online cost and competitive ratio
entries.text:
An online rule sees requests in arrival order. At time \(t\) it may use the observed prefix and its allowed internal state. The offline optimum knows the full sequence and obeys the resource and feasibility constraints specified for it. For a minimization problem, a typical competitive bound is \(\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+b\). The card says whether an additive constant is allowed and what it may depend on.

For a randomized rule and an oblivious adversary, the request sequence is fixed independently of the random bits. Expected cost is then taken for each such sequence. Random-order input, adaptive adversaries and regret against a fixed comparator define different guarantees.

entries.title: Streaming passes and memory
entries.text:
A stream supplies a sequence of records. A pass is one traversal in the stated order. In a one-pass algorithm, later computation can use an earlier record only through information saved when it was available. Space counts bits or words according to the card, including any retained seeds or buffers that its model charges.

An insertion-only stream, a stream with deletions and a uniformly random permutation of a fixed multiset give different inputs. Read the local convention for order, precision, success probability, permitted preprocessing and the size of the output.

entries.title: The cell-probe model
entries.text:
A data structure stores information in cells of \(w\) bits. A query may choose its next address using the query and values returned by earlier probes. Reading or writing a cell counts as a probe under the local rules. Computation between probes is free. Space counts available cells, or their bits if specified.

The card sets \(w\), the allowed preprocessing, private state, and any randomness. In a static problem the stored data do not change between queries. A dynamic problem specifies updates and whether the bound applies to each operation or is amortized over a sequence.

entries.title: Learning error, examples and confidence
entries.text:
For a classifier \(h\) and a joint law \(D\) of labeled examples, its zero-one error is \(\Pr_{(X,Y)\sim D}[h(X)\ne Y]\). In a realizable problem, the target class contains a hypothesis with zero error. An agnostic excess-error guarantee compares the output with the infimum of the error over the reference class. A proper learner must return a member of that class.

The confidence statement concerns the training sample and the learner's own randomness. The output's prediction error concerns a fresh draw from the specified distribution. The card fixes the sampling or query access, distribution family, loss, and whether time includes evaluating the returned hypothesis.

entries.title: Uniform quantum computation and BQP
entries.text:
A BQP computation decides a language using a uniform polynomial-size family of quantum circuits over a fixed efficiently specified universal gate set, with acceptance probability at least \(2/3\) on yes-inputs and at most \(1/3\) on no-inputs. Repetition with fresh work registers can reduce the error. The uniform constructor and input encoding are part of the model.

A quantum query counts an invocation of the specified oracle. A channel capacity, a quantum proof system and the distinguishing power of a restricted gate set each require their own resource and success definitions.

entries.title: Unit-cost string edit distance
entries.text:
For finite strings \(x,y\), their unit-cost edit distance is the smallest number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions that transform \(x\) into \(y\). Identical symbols may be matched at zero cost. Length counts symbols. The alphabet, representation, and the resource used to read each symbol are given locally.

An approximation to this distance, an edit script, and aligning more than two strings are different outputs. Tree edits and insertion/deletion-only metrics have their own local operations.

entries.title: Finite relational structures and conjunctive queries
entries.text:
A finite relational signature lists relation symbols and their arities. A structure interprets an \(r\)-ary symbol as a set of ordered \(r\)-tuples on its domain. A homomorphism maps elements of one structure into the other so that every tuple present in a relation maps to a tuple in the same relation. A conjunctive query existentially quantifies a conjunction of relational atoms, leaving any answer variables free.

Under set semantics a tuple is either present or absent. Under bag semantics occurrences carry multiplicity. Data complexity fixes the schema and query and varies the database. Combined complexity can include the query as input. The card specifies which objects vary, its access model and the semantics of constraints, answers or repairs.

entries.title: The SAT encoding for ETH and SETH
entries.text:
For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(b\) be the length of the binary expansion of \(a+1\). Define \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\,\operatorname{bin}(a+1)\). Codes are self-delimiting. With a fixed width bound \(q\ge3\), encode a CNF by \(\operatorname{code}(n)\), \(\operatorname{code}(m)\), then the \(m\) clauses in list order. A clause begins with its coded literal count. Each literal has a sign bit (zero for positive) and a coded index from \(1\) through \(n\). Every declared variable must occur. A clause may contain up to \(q\) literals, including zero. Repetitions and both signs of a variable are allowed. All lists must be complete and consume the entire input.

For a valid formula \(F\), \(n(F)\) counts its distinct variables and \(N(F)\) counts every encoded bit. On every valid formula, the uniform deterministic multitape machine must halt and decide satisfiability exactly. On malformed strings it must reject in time polynomial in their bit length. The running-time bound on valid formulas is the one in the display below. At each fixed \(q\), define \(s_q\) as the infimum of the \(\alpha\ge0\) for which some such machine and constants \(C\ge1\), \(d\in\mathbb N_0\) satisfy
\[t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(N(F)+1)^d\]
on every valid input. Testing all assignments shows \(0\le s_q\le1\). The machine and constants may depend on \(q,\alpha\). ETH concerns \(s_3\) and SETH concerns the limiting behavior as \(q\) grows.

entries.title: Certified numerical answers and infimum exponents
entries.text:
When a card asks for a numerical value \(x\) to absolute error \(\delta\), an answer \(a\) must come with a proof of \(|a-x|\le\delta\). One way is to prove \(\ell\le x\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le2\delta\), then take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). The answer must specify its value independently of the optimization, limit or unknown quantity the card asks to determine. For a function on a domain \(D\), supply one description of a function \(g\) and prove \(|g(t)-x(t)|\le\delta\) for every \(t\in D\). Two described bounding functions of pointwise width at most \(2\delta\) give such a \(g\) by their midpoint. An exact expression also qualifies. Each card specifies its own precision, any restriction on answer values, and its proof requirements. An interval may enclose an infimum or supremum even when no feasible object attains it.

For a growth exponent defined by \(x=\inf\{a:f(n)=O(n^a)\}\), the implicit constant and the threshold must obey the card’s uniformity requirements. The definition alone supplies neither an \(O(n^x)\) bound at the endpoint nor a limit for \(\log f(n)/\log n\).

entries.title: Synchronous LOCAL and CONGEST rounds
entries.text:
The communication network is a graph. Nodes run a distributed algorithm in synchronous rounds, exchanging messages with their neighbors. LOCAL permits arbitrarily long finite messages. CONGEST bounds the number of bits sent along each edge in each direction per round, typically by \(O(\log n)\) for \(n\) nodes. Local computation is unrestricted between rounds when the card specifies that convention.

The initial information, identifiers, shared or private randomness, and per-node outputs belong to the particular problem. A high-probability guarantee can concern one node or simultaneous correctness of all outputs. The statement specifies which event and which randomness the probability concerns.

cards.title: Simultaneous embedding with fixed edges for two graphs
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given any two finite simple planar graphs \(G_{1}=(V,E_{1})\) and \(G_{2}=(V,E_{2})\) on the same labeled vertex set, decides in polynomial time whether they admit planar topological drawings that coincide on every shared vertex and every shared edge?
cards.definitions: The input gives \(n\ge 0, V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), and two symmetric zero-diagonal \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrices, with total bit length N; each graph is promised planar. No drawing, vertex coordinates or embedding is supplied. The common graph is \(H=(V,E_{1}\cap E_{2})\), which may be disconnected and have isolated vertices. A drawing assigns distinct points \(p(v)\in \mathbb{R} ^{2}\) to vertices and to each edge uv a simple continuous arc with endpoints \(p(u),p(v)\), whose interior contains no vertex point. Planarity means that arcs for distinct edges of the same graph meet only at a common endpoint, if there is one. A simultaneous drawing uses the same \(p(v)\) in both graphs and exactly the same arc image for every edge in \(E_{1}\cap E_{2}\). Edges exclusive to different graphs may cross each other. Arcs may bend freely; no grid, edge-length, area or bend bound is imposed. The requested output is only YES or NO. Polynomial time means one always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants \(C,c\ge 1\) with at most \(C(N+1)^{c}\) bit steps on every promised input, with no oracle or advice. “Fixed edges” means shared drawings agree on their common edges, not that any geometry is fixed in the input.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that a polynomial-time decider exists for all promised pairs, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must cover arbitrary disconnected common graphs and freely chosen embeddings. A nonembeddable pair is a NO instance, not a refutation of polynomial decidability. Hardness for three input graphs, straight-line drawings or an additional optimization objective does not answer this question.

cards.context:
Think of two network diagrams whose vertices denote the same objects and whose edges describe two relations. Each view must be crossing-free on its own. Shared edges must stay in place when switching views. This is why drawing each graph independently can fail to meet the simultaneous requirement.

Take \(G_{1}\) to be \(K_{5}\) with one edge deleted and \(G_{2}\) to contain just that missing edge on the same five vertices. \(G_{1}\) is planar, and \(G_{2}\) can use the same vertex positions with its edge crossing edges exclusive to \(G_{1}\). This is a valid simultaneous drawing, even though the union is the nonplanar graph \(K_{5}\). Testing the union’s planarity would therefore reject valid instances.

The checked 2025 papers report polynomial-time algorithms when H is connected. This is connectivity of the shared edges and vertices, not merely connectivity of each input graph. Allowing H to have multiple components introduces compatibility of their positions as well as choices of embeddings, and the unrestricted two-graph question remains open in those sources.

Three-graph SEFE is NP-complete, but the number two is essential here. The March 2026 work on two paths studies straight-line grid drawings and optimizes geometric quantities. Its hardness result for edge length does not imply hardness of deciding whether unrestricted curved-edge drawings exist.

cards.title: Instance-optimal outer approximation of convex polytopes
cards.formal: Editorial finite-input variant: for every fixed \(d\ge2\), is there a deterministic algorithm which, given a full-dimensional polytope \(K\subseteq B_2^d\) by N vertices and \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), constructs a polytope P with \[K\subseteq P\subseteq K+\varepsilon B_2^d,\qquad f(P)\le C_d\operatorname{OPT}(K,\varepsilon),\] in time polynomial in N and \(1/\varepsilon\)? Here f counts facets and \(C_d\) depends only on dimension.
cards.definitions:
The input points have real coordinates, K is their convex hull, and \(B_2^d\) is the closed Euclidean unit ball centered at zero. The input promise is compactness, nonempty interior and containment in that ball; no lower bound on its inradius or minimum width is imposed. The Minkowski sum \(K+\varepsilon B\) consists of all \(x+\varepsilon u\) with \(x\in K\) and \(\|u\|_2\le1\). For an outer approximation this containment is equivalent to a Hausdorff error at most \(\varepsilon\).

\(\operatorname{OPT}(K,\varepsilon)\) is the minimum number of facets among all bounded full-dimensional real polytopes Q with \(K\subseteq Q\subseteq K+\varepsilon B\). Its comparator is allowed arbitrary real coefficients, not only input supporting hyperplanes. The algorithm outputs P as a finite list of real linear inequalities; redundant inequalities may be present but their number must also be at most \(C_d\operatorname{OPT}\). Facet count alone cannot hide an exponentially large output list. Use the exact-real RAM with +, −, ×, ÷, square roots, comparisons and memory operations at unit cost. All work and output writes are charged; there is no free convex-body optimization oracle. The algorithm, degree of its polynomial bound and approximation constant may depend on fixed d, but not K, N or \(\varepsilon\).

Choosing a finite vertex representation, a unit-radius normalization and polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) is an editorial specialization of the source’s broad request for an efficient instance-optimal construction. It does not claim polynomial bit complexity or an algorithm for arbitrary oracle-given convex bodies.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction with both containments, the instance-by-instance constant-factor output bound and the stated arithmetic time, or prove impossibility in this selected model. Bounds tight only for the worst body of a given volume or diameter do not establish the comparison with OPT for each input. A lower bound using an additional hypothesis settles impossibility only if that hypothesis is proved.

cards.title: FPT approximation of twin-width
cards.formal:
Do there exist total computable functions \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) and \(g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), an integer constant \(c\ge1\), and one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) such that, for every nonempty finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices and every integer \(k\ge0\), the machine halts within
\[
 f(k)(n+1)^c
\]
bit operations and either correctly reports \(\operatorname{tww}(G)>k\), or outputs a contraction sequence of \(G\) of width at most \(g(k)\)? Only the graph and \(k\) are supplied, with no helpful vertex order, decomposition or contraction sequence.
cards.definitions:
Here \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). The graph has vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\), and is given by its symmetric \(n\times n\) Boolean adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. The input also includes \(n\) and \(k\) in binary. Arbitrary disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. Vertex labels are just part of the explicit representation and carry no promise about a useful ordering.

A partition of \(V\) is a collection of pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets, called parts, whose union is \(V\). Two distinct parts \(X,Y\) form a mixed pair if there exist \(x,x'\in X\) and \(y,y'\in Y\) such that \(\{x,y\}\) is an edge of the original graph and \(\{x',y'\}\) is not. The two witness pairs need not have distinct endpoints within each part. A pair is not mixed when all possible cross pairs are edges, or when none are edges. Relations are always evaluated in the original graph.

For a partition \(\mathcal P\) and part \(X\in\mathcal P\), its red degree is
\[
 r_{\mathcal P}(X)=
 |\{Y\in\mathcal P\setminus\{X\}:(X,Y)\text{ is mixed}\}|.
\]
This counts mixed neighboring parts, not individual edges or vertices. Adjacency inside a part does not contribute to its red degree.

A contraction sequence is a list of partitions \(\mathcal P_n,\mathcal P_{n-1},\ldots,\mathcal P_1\). The first partition consists of all singleton vertices and the last is \(\{V\}\). Each \(\mathcal P_{j-1}\) is obtained from \(\mathcal P_j\) by merging exactly two distinct parts and leaving the others unchanged. The merged parts need not be adjacent. The width of a sequence is
\[
 \max_{1\le j\le n}\ \max_{X\in\mathcal P_j} r_{\mathcal P_j}(X).
\]
The twin-width \(\operatorname{tww}(G)\) is the minimum width over all such sequences. In particular, a one-vertex graph has width zero and its sequence has no merge steps.

The output encodes the \(n-1\) merges explicitly. Initially labels \(1,\ldots,n\) refer to singleton parts. At step \(t\), two distinct currently active labels are listed, their parts are replaced by their union, and the new part receives label \(n+t\). This list determines every partition and is a complete certificate, not just an upper-bound number or a promise that a sequence exists.

The two permitted outputs have the following meaning on every input. If the output is the rejection symbol, then \(\operatorname{tww}(G)>k\) must be true. If the output is a merge list, that list must always be a valid complete sequence of width at most \(g(k)\). Consequently, when \(\operatorname{tww}(G)\le k\) the machine must return a bounded-width sequence. When \(\operatorname{tww}(G)>k\), either output is allowed if its respective guarantee is true. There is no input promise that the parameter is an actual upper bound.

The deterministic machine has one finite program independent of \(k,n,G\), no advice and no oracle. The running time counts all bit-level computation, reading the binary parameter and the graph, constructing auxiliary information, and writing the output. The functions \(f\) and \(g\) are fixed total computable functions; their growth is unrestricted and may absorb the cost of reading the parameter. They depend only on \(k\), while the exponent \(c\) is a single constant independent of \(k\). No separate efficient evaluation bound on these functions is imposed, but any evaluation performed by \(A\) must fit the total running-time bound.

This is a fixed-parameter approximation with arbitrary computable width loss, not a specified multiplicative approximation ratio. A bound with a polynomial exponent depending on \(k\), such as \(n^{h(k)}\), is not the required fixed-parameter running time. Dependence on another graph parameter is insufficient unless it is bounded by a function of the supplied \(k\) on the inputs in question.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such \(A,f,g,c\) exist, including total computability of the functions, all-input termination, the running-time bound and both output guarantees, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation.

A negative answer must exclude all total computable width-loss functions and all fixed-parameter running-time bounds in the stated deterministic model. NP-hardness of exact recognition at a fixed twin-width, or a lower bound for a fixed approximation ratio, is not by itself such a negation: the card permits arbitrarily large computable \(g(k)\). A conditional result under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), ETH or another unproved assumption does not unconditionally decide the target.

An algorithm receiving a helpful ordering or a contraction sequence, restricted to one fixed width or a special graph class, or running in fixed-parameter time for a different unbounded structural parameter does not settle the whole statement without a proved extension.

cards.title: Near-logarithmic FPT inapproximability of Set Cover under Gap-ETH
cards.formal:
Does sparse deterministic Gap-ETH imply that, for some rational constant \(c>0\), no uniform deterministic FPT algorithm can distinguish
\[
\operatorname{OPT}(U,\mathcal S)\le k
\quad\text{from}\quad
\operatorname{OPT}(U,\mathcal S)>\rho_c(n)k,
\qquad
\rho_c(n)=\max\{1,c(\log_2(n+2))^{99/100}\},
\]
where \(n=|U|\) is the number of universe elements, \(\mathcal S\) is an explicitly given family of subsets of \(U\), and \(k\) is the parameter? FPT means time \(f(k)(L+1)^d\) for some computable function \(f\) and fixed exponent \(d\), with \(L\) the full input bit length. The two alternatives are promised; the definitions below fix the hypothesis and model.
cards.definitions:
A Set Cover instance consists of a universe \(U=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(n\ge1\), a list \(\mathcal S=(S_1,\ldots,S_M)\) of subsets of \(U\), and an integer \(1\le k\le\max\{1,M\}\). The sets need not be disjoint and may be empty or repeated. A cover is a set of indices \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,M\}\) with \(\bigcup_{j\in J}S_j=U\). Its cost is \(|J|\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}\) is the minimum cost, or \(+\infty\) if no cover exists. No disjoint-cover promise is imposed, even in the YES case.

Supply \(n,M,k\) in self-delimiting binary followed by the explicit \(n\)-by-\(M\) incidence matrix, in row order. For definiteness, a nonnegative integer \(z\) is coded by \(1^b0\) and then the \(b\)-bit expansion of \(z+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(z+1)\rfloor+1\). There is no trailing data. The total length is \(L\). The variable \(n\) in the approximation factor counts elements, not sets, incidences or encoding bits.

For fixed \(c\), an FPT gap algorithm means one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), an integer \(d\ge1\) and a total computable \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that every valid instance halts within \(f(k)(L+1)^d\) bit steps. It returns YES when \(\operatorname{OPT}\le k\), and NO when \(\operatorname{OPT}>\rho_c(n)k\). Between the two thresholds either answer is permitted, while the time bound still holds. All computation is charged, with no advice, randomness or oracle. A covering algorithm with the same parameterized time bound and guaranteed cost at most \(\rho_c(n)k\) whenever a size-\(k\) cover exists would in particular distinguish this gap.

Sparse deterministic Gap-ETH is the following proposition. There exist an integer \(B\ge1\) and rational constants \(\eta>0\) and \(0<\delta<1\) such that no deterministic uniform Turing machine, with any fixed constants \(K>0\) and integer \(q\ge1\), distinguishes satisfiable 3-CNF formulas from formulas whose assignments all satisfy at most a \(1-\delta\) fraction of clauses, in time
\[
K2^{\eta v}(\ell+1)^q.
\]
Here \(v\) is the number of occurring variables, there are at most \(Bv\) clauses, each clause contains at most three signed variables, and \(\ell\) is the full explicit binary clause-list encoding length. Encode counts, clause lengths and variable indices by the same self-delimiting integer code, with a sign bit for each literal. Clause occurrences count with multiplicity. The formula with no clauses has value one; an empty clause is false. Every declared variable must occur. The time bound holds for all valid formulas of this density, and either output is allowed outside the satisfiable-versus-gap promise. There is no randomness or advice in either hypothesis or conclusion.

The question is the implication from this hypothesis to \(\exists c>0\) with no FPT gap algorithm as defined above. It does not ask to prove Gap-ETH itself. The clipping of \(\rho_c\) at one only fixes small inputs and leaves the selected asymptotic factor unchanged.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed implication, with no unproved premise beyond its stated Gap-ETH antecedent, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive proof must justify the selected universe-size approximation factor and exclude every computable \(f(k)\) and fixed polynomial exponent in the stated deterministic model.

The logical negation requires Gap-ETH together with the existence, for every rational \(c>0\), of an FPT algorithm for the corresponding gap. Merely failing to prove a reduction or giving an approximation in time \(n^{g(k)}\) does not refute the implication. A lower bound using the number of candidate sets must justify its conversion to the universe-size convention. Hardness only for a factor depending on \(k\), a disjoint-cover promise or another optimization problem is not the selected target. Archival records the mathematical resolution reported in the checked source; it is not a claim that this Lean formalization has already been supplied.

Its significance is stronger approximation hardness under a fixed assumption, rather than weakening Gap-ETH itself.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Directed Feedback Vertex Set
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time constant-factor approximation for minimum-weight Directed Feedback Vertex Set on arbitrary finite directed graphs?

Precisely, do there exist one machine \(A\) and integers \(C,K,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid input \((D,w)\) of bit length \(N\), the machine halts within \(K(N+1)^d\) transitions and outputs a set \(F\subseteq V(D)\) satisfying
\[
D-F\text{ is acyclic},\qquad
\sum_{v\in F}w(v)\le C\,\operatorname{OPT}(D,w)?
\]
The same \(C,K,d,A\) must work for every graph and every allowed assignment of weights.
cards.definitions:
A directed graph is \(D=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge0\) and \(E\subseteq\{(u,v)\in[n]^2:u\ne v\}\). There are no loops or parallel copies of an arc, but both \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) may be present. There is no promise of planarity, bounded degree, bounded genus, quasi-transitivity or tournament structure.

A directed cycle consists of distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\), with \(r\ge2\), and arcs \((v_i,v_{i+1})\) for \(1\le i<r\) and \((v_r,v_1)\). The induced digraph \(D-F\) deletes the vertices in \(F\) and all their incident arcs. It is acyclic if it contains no directed cycle. A directed feedback vertex set is any \(F\) for which this holds. In particular, the two opposite arcs between a pair of vertices form a cycle.

Each vertex has a nonnegative rational weight \(w(v)\). Define
\[
\operatorname{OPT}(D,w)=
\min\left\{\sum_{v\in F}w(v):
F\subseteq[n]\text{ and }D-F\text{ is acyclic}\right\}.
\]
The minimum always exists because deleting all vertices is feasible. Zero weights are allowed. If the optimum is zero, the output must have weight zero as well; the guarantee has no additive slack. The empty graph has optimum zero.

For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(b(a)\) be the length of the ordinary binary expansion of \(a+1\), and encode \(a\) by \(1^{b(a)}0\) followed by those \(b(a)\) binary digits. Encode an instance by \(1^n0\), then the adjacency bits for all ordered pairs \((u,v)\), \(u\ne v\), in lexicographic order, then \(n\) pairs of integer codes \((p_v,q_v)\), where \(p_v\ge0\), \(q_v\ge1\) and \(w(v)=p_v/q_v\). A reduced fraction is not required. No trailing bits are allowed. All these bits contribute to \(N\); the running time may not depend polynomially on the numerical weights while ignoring their bit lengths.

The output is the \(n\)-bit incidence vector of an actual set \(F\). Feasibility is required on every input, as is the stated multiplicative cost guarantee. An estimate of the optimum without a feasible set, an expected-cost bound or a success probability below one is a different target.

The machine model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape, initially blank work tapes and an append-only output tape. A transition accesses the cells under the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. All transitions, including arithmetic, parsing and output, count toward the polynomial bound. There is no randomness, advice, oracle or uncharged preprocessing. Malformed encodings must be rejected in polynomial time. No complexity conjecture is assumed. Restricting the approximation constant to an integer loses nothing: any finite real factor can be rounded upward to an integer.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction of \(A,C,K,d\), proving polynomial bit complexity, feasibility and the constant-factor guarantee on every weighted digraph; or supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no such machine and constants exist. A conditional inapproximability theorem based on an unproved complexity conjecture does not establish the unconditional negative answer. An algorithm for a proper class of digraphs or for only unit weights does not establish the full positive answer. The target concerns existence of a fixed multiplicative approximation factor, not numerical estimation of the optimal possible factor.
cards.why: Deleting vertices to destroy every directed cycle is a basic optimization problem for cyclic dependencies. Its approximation behavior differs sharply from the undirected version: special directed graph classes admit constant factors, while the general case has resisted them and has strong conditional hardness. Resolving the unrestricted weighted target would clarify a central boundary of efficient approximation for directed graphs.

cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist one uniform randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, on every metric k-Median instance defined below, always outputs a nonempty facility set \(S\subseteq F\) with \(|S|\le k\), and satisfies \[\Pr\!\left[\operatorname{cost}(S)\le\left(1+\frac2e+\varepsilon\right)\operatorname{OPT}\right]\ge\frac23?\] Here \(e=\exp(1)\). The polynomial and program may depend on fixed \(\varepsilon\), but the running time must be polynomial in the full input length on every execution, with unrestricted input \(k\).
cards.definitions:
For the context, let \(\mathcal R\) be the set of fixed approximation factors achievable by the uniform randomized, always-feasible, worst-case polynomial-time algorithms below, with success probability at least \(2/3\) on each instance; let \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}=\inf\mathcal R\). Write \(e=\exp(1)\). 

An input is \(I=(v,C,F,k,d)\), with \(v\ge1\), \(V=[v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\), nonempty \(C,F\subseteq V\), \(C\cup F=V\), and an integer \(1\le k\le|F|\). The sets may overlap. The full table \(d:V\times V\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) is promised to be a metric: \(d(x,y)=d(y,x)\), \(d(x,y)=0\) if and only if \(x=y\), and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\) for all points. There are no weights or capacities: each client in \(C\) has unit demand, and facilities must be chosen from the supplied \(F\).

For a nonempty \(S\subseteq F\), let \[\operatorname{cost}(S)=\sum_{c\in C}\min_{s\in S}d(c,s),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}=\min_{S\subseteq F,\ 1\le|S|\le k}\operatorname{cost}(S).\] Both minima are over finite nonempty sets. The output need only specify the selected facilities; no assignment or optimality certificate is required. Feasibility is mandatory even on random executions where the approximation inequality fails. No extra facilities are allowed in such executions or merely on average. Zero optimum is included: in that case the successful executions must have exactly zero cost. In a metric this case occurs precisely when \(C\subseteq F\) and \(|C|\le k\); a quotient by the optimum is never used in the definition.

Fix a concrete binary encoding. For a nonnegative integer \(t\), write \(u(t)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\), where \(\operatorname{bin}\) has no leading zeros and \(a\) is its length. The input concatenates \(u(v)\), \(u(k)\), the two \(v\)-bit membership masks for \(C,F\), and the \(v^2\) rational entries in row-major order. An entry is a reduced pair \(p/q\) with integers \(p\ge0,q\ge1\), encoded by \(u(p)u(q)\); zero uses \(p=0,q=1\). The total length of this entire string is \(L\). A facility set is output as a \(v\)-bit membership mask. No bound on numerators or denominators is assumed beyond their finite encoding.

The model is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, a read-only input tape, initially blank work and output tapes, and ordinary charged tape transitions. A random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. Running time counts every transition, including preprocessing, arithmetic, random-bit generation and output; the stated polynomial bound holds on every random execution. There is no advice depending on input length, oracle, quantum operation or unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic. Behavior on strings outside the input promise is irrelevant. Success probability is over the random bits for each fixed input, not over an input distribution, and no single choice of coins must work for all inputs.

The factor \(r\) indexes an existence statement; it is not a real-valued input to the program. Different fixed factors may use different finite programs and polynomial constants. No computable rule converting an arbitrary real factor to a program is required. Both \(k\) and \(v\) vary within every such program’s input domain. Known constant-factor algorithms make \(\mathcal R\) nonempty, and \(\mathcal R\subseteq[1,\infty)\); hence its real infimum exists. The infimum need not be attained. No Euclidean, bounded-dimension, stability, sparsity or other additional promise is imposed.

cards.context:
The selected binary target is an algorithm for every factor \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed. This matches the familiar coverage-hardness scale from above without assuming that an algorithm attains the exact endpoint.

Metric k-Median chooses service locations and minimizes the sum of client travel distances. It also models selecting representatives for clustering. Clients and candidate facilities may be different sets, and the metric need not have Euclidean coordinates. The unresolved ratio measures how much optimization quality is lost when an arbitrary metric instance must be processed in polynomial time.

The known unconditional bounds give \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{med}}\le2\). The upper endpoint follows from the \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\); it does not assert a factor-two algorithm. Under \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), the coverage hardness below gives \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}\ge1+2/e\approx1.73576\). These are different kinds of bounds. In particular, \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would imply \(\rho_{\mathrm{med}}=1\).

Feige’s Theorem 5.3 gives an NP-hard coverage gap: all elements can be covered by \(k\) sets, or every such collection covers at most a \(1-1/e+\eta\) fraction, for any fixed \(\eta>0\). The associated client–facility metric uses separate copies of elements and sets, with cross distances one for incidence and three otherwise, and distance two between distinct points on the same side. Covering a fraction \(p\) corresponds to cost \((3-2p)|U|\), where \(U\) is the universe. Thus the gap becomes \(1\) versus \(1+2/e-2\eta\) per client.

This gap also explains the randomized assumption. A returned feasible solution of sufficiently small cost certifies the positive side; on a negative instance no such solution exists. Consequently a bounded-error algorithm beating the threshold would put the underlying NP-hard decision problem in \(\mathrm{RP}\), the class with polynomial time, one-sided error and no false acceptance. The exclusion for this card is therefore conditional on \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\), rather than justified by \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 Theorem 10 instead derives the classical k-Median lower bound from a Set Cover approximation barrier. The historical complexity assumption stated there is \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{DTIME}(n^{O(\log\log n)})\). Feige’s ordinary NP-hardness theorem for Max k-Cover and its metric gap distinguish the stronger coverage-based conclusion from the assumption in that earlier Set Cover argument.

Theorem 1.1 of the STOC 2025 paper, retained in its May 2026 full revision, gives a randomized polynomial-time \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation with a feasible facility budget. The separate Theorem 1.2 allows extra centers, but this is not the budget of the final theorem. Lemma 1.4 relates bounded integer distances to general distances, so the result is not confined to a fixed distance precision.

Byrka and coauthors’ April 2026 paper supplies another \((2+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for metric k-Median, in Corollary 1.2. Its intermediate guarantee opens \(k\) facilities only in expectation; the final approximation restores the facility budget with an \(\varepsilon\) loss. This distinction matters: an expected budget permits some outcomes with too many facilities and does not meet the card’s all-executions feasibility requirement. The new result does not narrow the interval between the known conditional lower endpoint and two.

The standard linear relaxation has fractional openings \(0\le y_s\le1\), assignments \(0\le x_{c,s}\le y_s\), \(\sum_s x_{c,s}=1\) for every client, and \(\sum_s y_s\le k\), minimizing \(\sum_{c,s}d(c,s)x_{c,s}\). Its integrality gap approaches two. For a unit-edge star with \(q\ge3\) leaves, all vertices as facilities, leaves as clients and \(k=q-1\), the integral optimum is two. A feasible fractional solution has center opening \(1/(q-1)\), each leaf opening \((q-2)/(q-1)\), and each client assigned to its own leaf and the center in those proportions. Its cost is \(q/(q-1)\), yielding a gap at least \(2(q-1)/q\). This is a barrier for that relaxation, not an unconditional computational lower bound against the true integral optimum.

Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 Theorem 1 attains \(1+2/e+\varepsilon\) in time \(f(k,\varepsilon)n^{O(1)}\). That fixed-parameter guarantee allows a dependence on \(k\) which need not be polynomial. Here \(k\) is part of the unrestricted input, so the parameterized result does not establish the corresponding polynomial-time factor.

The March 2026 low-dimensional Euclidean work improves approximation-scheme running times by using geometric structure. Its guarantees do not apply to arbitrary metric tables.

The July 2026 spectral dual-fitting preprint improves k-Means guarantees in Euclidean and general metrics. That objective sums squared distances, which changes both approximation and hardness constants; the paper does not give a smaller general k-Median ratio.

The requested approximation must refer to the same input class, randomness convention and facility budget. A fixed-parameter runtime, a relaxation-gap example or a guarantee opening extra facilities does not establish this polynomial-time upper bound.

cards.title: Breaking factor two for precedence-constrained makespan
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, for every instance of nonpreemptive precedence-constrained scheduling on identical parallel machines, outputs a feasible schedule \(S\) with \[C_{\max}(S)\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}?\] Processing times are positive binary-encoded integers, the precedence graph is arbitrary and acyclic, and the number of machines is part of the input. The constant \(\varepsilon\) cannot depend on the instance. No complexity assumption is imposed.
cards.definitions:
For context, let \(\mathcal R\) be the real factors achieved by a uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm on every valid instance, and let \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=\inf\mathcal R\). 

Instance. There are jobs \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\), positive integer processing times \(p_j\), a positive integer machine count \(m\), and a directed acyclic graph \(D=(J,F)\). An arc \((i,j)\in F\) requires job \(i\) to finish before job \(j\) starts. Every arc is a requirement; its transitive consequences also hold. There is no promise on the shape or depth of the directed acyclic graph, and the machine count is not fixed in advance. Every job may run on every machine, and every machine takes exactly \(p_j\) units of time to process job \(j\).

Schedule and feasibility. A schedule specifies for each job a machine \(a_j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and a nonnegative start time \(s_j\). The job occupies precisely the half-open interval \([s_j,s_j+p_j)\) on that machine. Intervals on the same machine must be pairwise disjoint, and
\[s_j\ge s_i+p_i\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in F.\]
Execution is continuous and uninterrupted: no job may be split, preempted or migrated. Finishing one job and starting another at the same instant is allowed. All jobs are available initially subject to their precedences. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup times, machine eligibility restrictions or other resource constraints. The schedule uses the same number of unit-speed machines as the optimum; extra machines or speed are not allowed.

Objective. The makespan is the latest completion time,
\[C_{\max}(S)=\max_{j\in J}(s_j+p_j),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{S\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(S).\]
This is elapsed time from zero, not the sum or average of completion times. The optimum is positive and at most \(W=\sum_j p_j\). It is unchanged if start times are restricted to nonnegative integers: for any feasible schedule, retain its machine assignments and within-machine job orders and start each job as early as those orders and the precedences allow. Positive integer durations give an acyclic augmented order and integral earliest starts without increasing the makespan. Thus an optimal integer schedule exists. Having more than \(n\) machines offers no advantage, although the full encoded value of \(m\) is counted in the input length.

Encoding. For an integer \(i\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(i+1\) and set \(U(i)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(i+1)\), with exactly \(\ell\) bits in the last part. Encode an instance as \(U(n)U(m)U(p_1)\cdots U(p_n)\) followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits of \(D\) in row-major order. Valid inputs have the stated positivity and acyclicity properties. Encode an output schedule as the list \(U(a_1)U(s_1)\cdots U(a_n)U(s_n)\), with integer starts. These are explicit binary data, not succinct circuits or value oracles. All output bits and arithmetic costs count.

Algorithms and ratios. Computation uses a finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet, no advice, oracle or random bits. Polynomial time is measured in the full bit length \(N\), including all durations and the machine count, not in the numeric sum of processing times. Invalid encodings may be rejected. Each algorithm defining membership in \(\mathcal R\) must halt within its fixed polynomial bound on all valid inputs and always output a feasible schedule. Its factor \(r\) must hold simultaneously for every job count, machine count, positive duration vector and precedence graph. The program and polynomial may depend on the fixed factor \(r\), but cannot be chosen separately for each instance size. No accuracy parameter is supplied to that program in this definition.

The infimum. Graham’s polynomial-time list-scheduling guarantee implies \(2\in\mathcal R\), while feasibility forces all ratios to be at least one. Hence \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\). The real infimum is defined even if no algorithm attains it. In particular, proving \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le u\) may establish algorithms with ratios arbitrarily close to \(u\) from above; it need not exhibit an algorithm with ratio exactly \(u\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that some fixed improvement \(\varepsilon>0\) over factor two is attainable by one deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm on every allowed precedence instance, or refute this for every fixed improvement.
cards.why: Precedence constraints make scheduling depend on both how much work can run in parallel and which completions unlock later jobs. The optimal approximation ratio measures the algorithmic cost of coordinating these two effects. Pinning it down would settle a central scheduling approximation boundary whose basic factor-two guarantee dates to the 1960s.

references.title: Inapproximability of Unique-Machine Precedence Scheduling for Unit-Length Jobs
references.authors: Venkatesan Guruswami; Xuandi Ren; Shaoxuan Tang
references.locator: Version 1, 29 July 2026. Full introduction and Theorems 1.2–1.3 inspected. Each job has a predetermined eligible machine; this different model is explicitly contrasted with unrestricted identical-machine assignment.

cards.context:
The input is an entire task graph, not a stream of arrivals. A scheduler may inspect all durations and dependencies before choosing assignments and start times. It must place every job, keep each job uninterrupted, and minimize the last completion time. Changing to an online rule, preemption, machine-dependent durations or total completion time changes the problem.

Total work \(W=\sum_j p_j\) gives the lower bound \(W/m\) on any feasible makespan. The total duration \(D\) of a longest directed path in the precedence graph gives another lower bound, since that chain runs sequentially. The difficulty is that filling machines now and finishing jobs that unlock future work can call for different priorities.

Graham’s list scheduling starts available jobs according to a priority order when machines become free. A job is available after all its predecessors finish. The established bound is \(C_{\max}\le W/m+(1-1/m)D\le(2-1/m)\operatorname{OPT}\). Although this is below two for each finite \(m\), its supremum over input machine counts is two. It therefore gives the universal bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\), not a fixed improvement below two.

A priority example separates a poor list from algorithmic impossibility. For \(m\ge2\), take \(m(m-1)\) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length \(m\). Listing the long job last gives makespan \(2m-1\), whereas starting it immediately and distributing the units over the other machines gives makespan \(m\), which also equals the work lower bound. This shows tightness for that list order; it has no precedence edges and does not prove hardness for every algorithm.

Classical NP-hardness excludes every factor strictly below \(4/3\) unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Consequently \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) implies \(4/3\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\). The word “unless” is essential: NP-hardness is not an unconditional proof that a polynomial-time algorithm cannot exist.

The binary target asks whether \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}<2\). A strict inequality is equivalent to an actual fixed-factor improvement; there is no endpoint-attainment issue at a value strictly below two.

Svensson proves a transfer from the approximability of a different objective: total weighted completion time on a single machine with precedences. Hardness arbitrarily close to two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit jobs. The transferred loss tends to zero, but the two scheduling objectives and their approximation parameters are not identical.

His Corollary 1 uses the Bansal–Khot Unique Games variant in Appendix Hypothesis 1. It requires a satisfiable large bipartite portion in the completeness case and an extra expansion condition in the soundness case. The paper explicitly distinguishes it from ordinary UGC and does not establish their equivalence. Together with P different from NP, this hypothesis gives inapproximability for every fixed factor below two and hence the conditional value two.

The infimum asks which ratios can be approached by finite uniform algorithms. It need not have a minimizing algorithm: \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=1\), for example, would not by its definition alone assert an exact polynomial-time optimizer. Similarly, an upper bound on the infimum can be witnessed by algorithms approaching that bound. The prescribed \(1/100\) accuracy concerns the real threshold, not the approximation error of one submitted scheduling algorithm.

The selected question concerns the existence of a universal fixed improvement below two. A conditional inapproximability result supplies only a conditional negative answer unless its assumption is also proved.

Nederlof, Swennenhuis and Węgrzycki give an exact unit-job algorithm running in \((1+n/m)^{O(\sqrt{nm})}\) time; this is subexponential when \(m=o(n)\). They also improve the exponential base in the regime \(m=\Theta(n)\). The work appeared at SODA 2025 and online in TALG in January 2026. Faster exact exponential-time algorithms do not supply a polynomial-time universal approximation ratio.

The July 2026 unique-machine preprint proves NP-hardness of every constant approximation factor for unit jobs when each job has one predetermined eligible machine. This removes assignment flexibility and is an additional input restriction on allowable schedules, absent from the present model. Its stronger hardness therefore does not contradict the factor-two algorithm for freely assignable identical machines.

The selected question asks whether some fixed positive improvement below factor two is possible in polynomial time. A qualifying algorithm settles it even if the optimal approximation ratio remains unknown. A negative answer requires an unconditional impossibility theorem; a conditional hardness statement must retain its hypothesis.

cards.formal: For critical four-state Swendsen–Wang dynamics on the square torus of side \(L\ge3\), do there exist absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le C L^c\) for every \(L\)?
cards.definitions:
The graph has vertex set \((\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^2\) with distinct vertices adjacent exactly when one coordinate differs by \(1\) or \(-1\) modulo \(L\) and the other agrees. Duplicate edges are suppressed. A configuration \(\sigma\) assigns one of \(q\) colors to each vertex. At inverse temperature \(\beta\), its probability is proportional to \(\exp(\beta\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}\mathbf 1\{\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)\})\). There is no external field.

One step independently keeps each monochromatic edge with probability \(p=1-e^{-\beta}\), drops every other edge, and gives each connected component an independent uniform color. Isolated vertices are components. In this normalization \(\beta_c(q)=\log(1+\sqrt q)\). Take \(q=4\), \(\beta=\log 3\), and \(p=2/3\). Use [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) at tolerance \(1/4\), counting whole Swendsen–Wang updates.
