cards.title: Strongly polynomial near-linear negative-weight shortest paths
cards.formal:
Do there exist one uniform classical randomized comparison-addition algorithm \(A\), constants \(C>0\), integers \(k\ge0\) and \(B\ge3\), and a polynomial \(p\) with the following property? For every directed graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices, \(m\) arcs, arbitrary real arc lengths and no negative directed cycle, and every specified source \(s\), every execution of \(A\) halts within
\[
 C(m+n)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^k
\]
instructions in the model below, and with probability at least \(2/3\) outputs all exact distances from \(s\)? The bound is uniform over all graph densities and real weight assignments and is independent of numerical magnitude or encoding length. On rational inputs the additional encoding-space bound is \(p(N)\), where \(N\) is the full binary input length.
cards.definitions:
The input contains the vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a source \(s\in V\), and an explicit ordered list \(E\) of \(m\) directed arcs with their real lengths \(\lambda_e\in\mathbb R\). There are no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Thus \(0\le m\le n(n-1)\). Isolated vertices and disconnected graphs are allowed. Lengths may be positive, zero or negative and are otherwise unrestricted.

The length of a finite directed walk is the sum of its traversed arc lengths, counting repeated arcs. The empty walk from a vertex to itself has length zero. The promise is that every directed cycle in the entire graph has nonnegative total length, including cycles unreachable from \(s\). For each vertex \(v\), define
\[
 d(s,v)=\inf\left\{\sum_{e\in P}\lambda_e:
                 P\text{ is a directed walk from }s\text{ to }v\right\}.
\]
If no such walk exists, the output is a distinguished \(+\infty\) marker. Otherwise the promise makes the value finite, attained by a simple path (or the empty path when \(v=s\)). In particular \(d(s,s)=0\). The algorithm must explicitly output all \(n\) entries in vertex order, with exact real values for reachable vertices. Reporting a negative cycle is not an alternative valid answer on a promised input. Behavior outside the negative-cycle promise is not part of the requested guarantee.

The machine is a comparison-addition RAM with exact real cells and unsigned control/address words of
\[
 w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil
\]
bits. Input arcs, endpoints and lengths initially occupy explicit memory cells. The program is finite and fixed for all sizes, with only finitely many fixed rational constants. It has no nonuniform advice, input-dependent precomputed table or numerical-encoding oracle. Unused memory initially contains zero.

On real cells the unit-cost operations are reading, writing, copying, addition, subtraction and exact comparison. No multiplication or division of real values, floor, bit extraction or conversion of an input-dependent real value into a word is available. Real cells cannot be used as addresses. The infinity output is a tagged marker, not a real on which unrestricted arithmetic is allowed.

Word operations have unit cost: reads, writes, copies, comparisons, branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) positions return zero. Word arithmetic cannot inspect or operate on an encoding of a real cell. Multiword calculations cost their component instructions. A fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one instruction; all generated random words are independent. Every used address must fit in one word.

All computation is charged, including memory access, control, preprocessing, random generation and output. The time bound holds for each promised input and every random execution, including those producing an incorrect answer. Correctness is the joint event that the complete distance vector and all unreachable markers are correct, with probability at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input. Deterministic algorithms are included.

On rational inputs, encode each real input length by a binary numerator and positive denominator, and let \(N\) count these bits together with the entire graph description. Every stored rational, written in reduced form, must have numerator and denominator lengths at most \(p(N)\), and the total bit space used to represent all cells and control words must also be at most \(p(N)\), on every execution. This additional condition is separate from the arithmetic operation count. No finite encoding is imposed on an arbitrary real input; the comparison-addition operations specify how it can be accessed.

The program and \(C,k,B,p\) are chosen once and cannot depend on the graph, source, weight values or their ordering. The term near-linear in this card means the displayed fixed polylogarithmic overhead over \(m+n\). It is not the weaker overhead \((m+n)^{o(1)}\). Restricting lengths to bounded integers or requiring all lengths to be nonnegative changes the task.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated algorithm's existence or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation.

A positive answer must establish exactness of the entire output, the per-input success probability, worst-case comparison-addition cost for arbitrary real lengths, and polynomial encoding space on rational inputs. It must cover sparse as well as dense graphs. A deterministic algorithm with these bounds qualifies.

A negative answer must exclude every admissible uniform algorithm and every fixed polylogarithmic exponent in this model. A lower bound for one particular framework or a conditional result under an unproved conjecture does not establish that negation. An integer-weight algorithm whose operation count depends on weight magnitude, an almost-quadratic bound independent of m, or a merely approximate-distance algorithm is insufficient without a proved extension meeting the full target.

cards.title: Single-exponential exact cut mimicking networks
cards.formal:
Does there exist an absolute real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E,w)\) with finite nonnegative real edge weights and every specified terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) of size \(k\ge2\), there is a finite simple undirected graph \(H=(V_H,E_H,w_H)\) with nonnegative real edge weights such that
\[
 T\subseteq V_H,\qquad |V_H|\le2^{Ck},\qquad
 \forall\,\varnothing\ne A\subsetneq T,\quad
 \lambda_{H,T}(A)=\lambda_{G,T}(A)?
\]
Here the terminal cut value is
\[
 \lambda_{G,T}(A)=
 \min_{\substack{S\subseteq V\\ S\cap T=A}}
 \sum_{e\in\delta_G(S)}w(e),
\]
and the analogous formula defines \(\lambda_{H,T}\). The replacement graph is arbitrary and need not be a contraction, minor or subgraph of \(G\).
cards.definitions:
A simple undirected graph has edges that are unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with no loops or parallel edges. For \(S\subseteq V\), the set \(\delta_G(S)\) contains exactly the edges with one endpoint in \(S\) and the other in \(V\setminus S\). Its cut value is the sum of their weights. Every weight is a finite element of \(\mathbb R_{\ge0}\); zero weights, disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. There are no infinite or negative capacities.

The elements of \(T\) are distinct labelled terminals. In the minimization defining \(\lambda_{G,T}(A)\), all terminals of \(A\) must lie on one side and all terminals of \(T\setminus A\) on the other; nonterminals may be placed on either side to minimize the total. The feasible family of sides is finite and nonempty, so the minimum exists. In an undirected graph the values for \(A\) and \(T\setminus A\) coincide. Zero values must be preserved exactly as well.

The graph \(H\) contains the same labelled terminals, without merging any two of them. Its other vertices and all its weights may be chosen freely as functions of \(G,w,T\). There is no required map from original nonterminals to replacement vertices and no requirement to retain original edges. Parallel edges in an alternative representation can be combined by adding their weights, and loops can be removed, so restricting the representation to simple graphs does not change these cut values.

Preservation is simultaneous: one graph \(H\) must satisfy the equality for every nonempty proper terminal subset. It preserves the minimum cut values, not the identities of individual minimum cuts or a correspondence between all graph cuts. Preserving only a minimum cut between each terminal pair is a weaker requirement, since other terminals are then free to move to either side. Preserving all multicommodity flow demands is a different, stronger request not imposed here.

Size means the number of vertices of \(H\), including all \(k\) terminals. No independent edge-count or bit-length bound is requested, and real weights need not be rational or have an effective finite encoding. This is an existence question, with no algorithmic or construction-time requirement. The constant \(C\) precedes all graphs, weights and terminal counts; it cannot vary with an instance. The requested bound is \(2^{O(k)}\) with a linear exponent, not merely \(2^{\operatorname{poly}(k)}\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of such a common constant \(C\) and exact replacement graphs, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation.

A positive proof must cover all finite nonnegatively real-weighted undirected graphs and all terminal bipartitions using a single replacement graph for each instance. A negative proof must defeat every proposed \(C\), allowing arbitrary new vertices and arbitrary nonnegative real weights. Lower bounds confined to contractions, approximations, pairwise cuts or a prescribed class of replacement graphs do not refute this statement. A bound with a superlinear polynomial exponent does not establish the requested upper bound. No numerical tolerance or unproved computational assumption is part of acceptance.

cards.title: Logarithmic fully retroactive priority queues
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic comparison pointer-machine program \(A\), with fixed constants \(C_t,C_s>0\), that implements the fully retroactive priority queue defined below on every valid finite sequence of commands? Starting with an empty history, it must insert and remove historical insertion or extract-min records, and return the minimum item immediately after any queried historical time. Write \(m_j\) for the number of historical records after command \(j\), \(m_0=0\), and \(M_j=\max\{m_{j-1},m_j\}\). For every \(q\ge0\), require
\[
T_A(q)\le C_t\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\log_2(2+M_j)\right),
\]
where \(T_A(q)\) counts initialization and all steps through the first \(q\) commands. During command \(j\), at most \(C_s(1+M_j)\) records may be allocated and not yet reclaimed; after it finishes, at most \(C_s(1+m_j)\) may remain. Initialization uses at most \(C_s\) records. Thus time is amortized over all edits and queries, while space is linear in the currently maintained history, including working storage.
cards.definitions:
Fix three opaque totally ordered domains: priorities, item identities and historical times. The same program and constants must work for every choice of these domains and every valid input sequence. An item is a pair \((p,\iota)\) of priority and identity, ordered lexicographically: compare priorities first and use identities to break ties. Identities of items whose insertion records are currently in the history are distinct. Atoms in each domain can be copied and compared in constant time, with no access to their representation.

The history is a finite set of records with pairwise distinct timestamps. A record is either \(\operatorname{InsertItem}(t,p,\iota)\) or \(\operatorname{ExtractMin}(t)\). Its meaning is obtained by sorting the records by time and replaying them from an empty queue. An insertion adds its item; an extraction removes the least surviving item in the lexicographic order. The history after every edit is promised valid: no extraction is encountered with an empty queue. There is no monotonicity promise on priorities. The data structure need not detect invalid commands or histories.

An input command has one of four forms. \(\operatorname{AddInsert}(t,p,\iota)\) adds an insertion record at an unused timestamp. \(\operatorname{AddExtract}(t)\) adds an extraction record at an unused timestamp. Either addition returns a constant-size stable handle for the new historical record. \(\operatorname{Remove}(h)\) removes the existing historical record named by its valid handle; a handle becomes invalid after that removal. \(\operatorname{Minimum}(t)\) returns the identity and priority of the least item after replaying all current records with timestamp at most \(t\), or a distinguished empty marker. The supplied query time may coincide with a record, lie between records, or precede or follow all records. Thus an insertion at \(t\) is already effective at \(t\), and an extraction at \(t\) has already removed its item. Edits change the interpretation of all subsequent historical records. An extraction record is not a request to remove a named item, and a removal command deletes a historical operation rather than executing an extra queue extraction.

The computation is online: each command arrives only after the preceding response, and its response must be completed before the next command is seen. Commands may depend on earlier responses. Input atoms and a removal handle occupy only constantly many input registers; earlier inputs remain available to the program only if it stores them in its charged memory. The client may retain returned handles, but gives the program only the handle named by the current command, with no auxiliary stored computation.

A program has finite control and a fixed finite number of registers. Memory consists of records with a fixed finite number of pointer fields and data fields. A pointer is null or the address of an allocated record. A data field contains one input atom or a symbol from a fixed finite alphabet. Each step may read or write a fixed field of a record reached by a register, copy a register or field, follow a stored pointer, compare two pointers for equality, compare two atoms from the same ordered domain, test a finite-alphabet symbol, branch, allocate or reclaim one record, or emit one output field. Each such primitive costs one step. Allocation supplies a fresh available address; addresses cannot be ordered, converted to data, used in arithmetic, or used for computed array access. Pointer access starts from the fixed registers or follows stored pointers. Unbounded integers and bit strings, if needed, must be represented by charged records and manipulated through these primitives; there is no unit-cost arithmetic on counters. There are no random bits, advice, oracle operations or uncharged preprocessing.

Every allocated record counts toward space until reclaimed, including historical records, handle records, indexes, temporary storage and unreachable garbage. Rebuilding and reclamation count toward time. The parameters \(m_j,M_j\) are used to state the guarantee and are not free machine inputs or unit-cost counters. A query does not change \(m_j\), and an edit changes it by exactly one. The bounds hold for every finite prefix, including arbitrarily long sequences that repeatedly add and remove records while keeping the current history small. They do not use the cumulative number of commands as a replacement for history size. The record format, register count, program and resource constants are fixed independently of all inputs.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a uniform deterministic implementation and constants satisfying the exact replay semantics, total-prefix time bound and space bounds for every valid command sequence, or a complete Lean proof of their logical negation in the stated comparison pointer-machine model. All representation, correctness and resource claims must be included. A conditional lower bound alone does not establish unconditional nonexistence, and a result confined to monotonic histories or using a different machine model does not settle this target.

cards.title: Polynomial-time computation of addition-chain length
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(K>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N\) and one deterministic multitape Turing machine that, on every positive integer \(n\) supplied in binary, outputs the exact shortest addition-chain length \(\ell(n)\) in binary within \(K(b+1)^a\) steps, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\) is the input length?
cards.definitions:
An addition chain for \(n\ge1\) is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers
\[
1=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_r=n
\]
such that for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there exist indices \(j,k\in\{0,\ldots,i-1\}\) with \(a_i=a_j+a_k\). The two indices may coincide, and an earlier entry may be reused any number of times. The length is the number \(r\) of additions, not the number \(r+1\) of entries. Define \(\ell(n)\) as the minimum such length; in particular, \(\ell(1)=0\). The only initially available number is \(1\). Subtraction, division, multiplication of chain entries and additional initial constants are not chain operations. The sum need not use the immediately preceding entry.

The machine receives just the ordinary binary expansion of \(n\), with no leading zeros. Its output is the ordinary binary expansion of the integer \(\ell(n)\), with \(0\) written as a single zero bit. The same finite program and constants must work for all valid inputs. The program has the usual unrestricted finite alphabet and binary work tapes of a multitape Turing machine, but all work, input reads and output writing count in its worst-case step bound. It has no advice, oracle, random bits or uncharged preprocessing. Invalid input strings must be rejected within the same bound with \(b\) interpreted as their string length. No addition chain or auxiliary number-theoretic data are supplied.

The requested machine may use any deterministic computation to find the length; the restrictions on chain operations define the quantity being optimized, rather than restricting the machine's internal calculations. The output is only the optimal length, not a chain attaining it. The input is a single binary target, not a list of targets and not a unary string of length \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm and fixed polynomial bound satisfying the exact-output task for every \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. Exact integer output is part of this computational existence question, not an extra accuracy restriction on a numerical-value benchmark. A fast approximation, a heuristic, polynomial time in \(n\) instead of its bit length, or a result for special targets does not meet the stated guarantee. Hardness for a single target under an additional hypothesis settles the negative answer only with a proof of that hypothesis. Hardness for several prescribed targets addresses a different input problem.
cards.why: Addition chains express reuse in multiplication-only exponentiation. Their optimal length is small enough to have short certificates, yet finding that length for an arbitrary binary exponent has resisted a general complexity classification.

cards.title: Explicit rigidity at rank n over log log n
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\), constants \(K>0\), \(b\in\mathbb N\), and one deterministic Turing machine which, for every integer \(n\ge4\), outputs a matrix \(A_n\in\mathbb F_2^{n\times n}\) within \(Kn^b\) steps, such that
\[
\forall c>0\ \exists N_c\ge4\ \forall n\ge N_c:
R_{A_n}^{\mathbb F_2}\!\left(
\min\!\left\{n,\left\lfloor\frac{cn}{\log_2\log_2 n}\right\rfloor\right\}
\right)\ge n^{1+\varepsilon}?
\]
Here \(c\) is real, \(N_c,n\) are integers, and \(R^{\mathbb F_2}\) is the minimum number of entries that must be changed to reduce rank to the indicated value. The same matrix family and the same \(\varepsilon\) must work for every fixed \(c\).
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) uses addition and multiplication modulo 2. For a matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{n\times n}\) and an integer \(0\le r\le n\), define
\[
R_A^{\mathbb F_2}(r)=
\min\left\{
\bigl|\{(i,j):A_{ij}\ne B_{ij}\}\bigr|:
B\in\mathbb F_2^{n\times n},\ \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}(B)\le r
\right\}.
\]
Rank is the dimension of the column span over \(\mathbb F_2\), not over the reals. Every entry of \(B\) can be chosen independently. The cost counts changed positions in the whole matrix, not a maximum or average per row, a norm of the changes, or their numerical magnitude. The minimum exists because the candidate set is finite and contains the zero matrix. This is ordinary matrix rigidity, not a separately constrained row/column version.

The construction algorithm receives \(1^n\) and outputs all \(n^2\) bits of \(A_n\), in row-major order, on a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine. Its time bound includes writing those bits. It has no random bits, advice, noncomputable constants or oracle access. It outputs one matrix at each length, rather than a list containing an unspecified rigid member. Polynomial time in \(n\) is required; logarithmic-time computation of an individual entry is not additionally required.

All logarithms in the rank threshold are base 2. For \(n\ge4\), the iterated logarithm is positive. The minimum with \(n\) makes the rank parameter valid even before the eventual guarantee begins. For each fixed \(c\), sufficiently large \(n\) have \(\log_2\log_2 n>c\), so the clipping eventually disappears. The threshold length \(N_c\) may depend on \(c\); the algorithm, \(K,b\) and \(\varepsilon\) may not. The comparison with \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) is an ordinary real inequality against an integer rigidity value, equivalently a lower bound by its ceiling.

The target is unconditional existence of an explicit family and a proof of its rigidity. The algorithm is not required to compute rigidity or output a certificate with each matrix. The same \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed for the whole family, with no prescribed numerical lower bound such as \(1/100\). A rank guarantee for just one fixed \(c\), or for ranks much smaller than \(n/\log\log n\), is not the quantified target here.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the explicit-family existence statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify and verify the deterministic construction and prove the rigidity inequality against every binary matrix of the allowed rank, for all fixed \(c\) and all sufficiently large lengths. A random-matrix existence proof, an unselected candidate list, an oracle construction, a conditional construction, or a rigidity bound over a different field is insufficient. A negative answer must exclude all constructions with the stated properties, not merely refute a familiar proposed family.
cards.why: A sufficiently rigid explicit binary matrix gives a linear transformation whose computation resists linear-size logarithmic-depth circuits. Random matrices have strong rigidity, but obtaining the required guarantees from a uniform deterministic construction remains a central explicit lower-bound challenge.

cards.title: VP factor closure in positive characteristic
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{VP}_{F}\) closed under polynomial factors for every field \(F\) of positive characteristic? Explicitly, quantify first over every prime \(p\), every field \(F\) with \(\operatorname{char}(F)=p\), every function \(m:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N\), and every two polynomial families
\[
f_n,g_n\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\qquad(n\ge1).
\]
Does the following implication always hold?
\[
\begin{split}
&\left[\ \forall n\ge1,\ f_n\ne0\text{ and }g_n\mid f_n\ \right]\\
&\quad\land\left[\ \exists A,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,\
\max\{m(n),\deg(f_n),L_F(f_n)\}\le A(n+1)^k\ \right]\\
&\qquad\Longrightarrow\left[\ \exists B,\ell\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,\
L_F(g_n)\le B(n+1)^{\ell}\ \right]?
\end{split}
\]
Here \(L_F\) is exact algebraic circuit size as defined below, and degree means total degree. The field is fixed throughout each family. Constants in the polynomial bounds may depend on the field and the families but not on \(n\). There is no restriction on factor multiplicities, including multiplicities divisible by \(p\).
cards.definitions:
A field has characteristic \(p\) when \(p\) is the smallest positive integer such that the sum of \(p\) copies of \(1_F\) is zero. The statement includes finite and infinite fields, including fields that are not perfect or algebraically closed. A field of characteristic \(p\) is perfect if every element has a \(p\)-th root in that same field. This property is not an assumption of the question.

The variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}\) commute. Polynomial equality and divisibility are identities in the formal polynomial ring over \(F\), not equality only as functions on \(F^{m(n)}\). Thus \(g_n\mid f_n\) means that some \(h_n\in F[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\) satisfies the identity \(f_n=g_nh_n\). The requirement \(f_n\ne0\) implies that both factors are nonzero. Constant factors and the whole polynomial are allowed. For a nonzero polynomial, total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient; nonzero constants have degree zero. The ring with zero variables is \(F\). Since \(F\) is a field and \(f_n\ne0\), a divisor has total degree at most \(\deg(f_n)\).

An algebraic circuit over \(F\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output gate. An input gate is labeled by a variable or by any element of \(F\). Every other gate has two ordered input positions, each referencing an earlier gate in a topological ordering, and is labeled by addition or multiplication. A predecessor may be used in both input positions. Fan-out is unrestricted, and the same intermediate polynomial may be reused. Evaluation is formal addition and multiplication in \(F[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\). The circuit size is the total number of gates, including variable and constant gates. The quantity \(L_F(u)\) is the minimum such size among circuits computing \(u\) exactly.

No division, root-extraction, oracle or approximation gates are allowed. Arbitrary constants from the fixed base field each occupy one constant gate; their bit descriptions or computability are not charged. This is algebraic size complexity, not bit complexity. A circuit can equivalently be recorded as a topologically ordered finite list of gate labels and predecessor indices. The representation carries actual field elements as labels and is not required to encode them as finite binary strings. There is no restriction on circuit depth or on degrees of intermediate gates, and no randomness or permitted error in the circuit's output.

A family belongs to \(\mathrm{VP}_{F}\) when its number of variables, output total degree and minimum circuit size have polynomial bounds in the family index, precisely as in the antecedent. The circuits for distinct indices may be unrelated: neither the circuit family nor its field constants must be generated uniformly. The desired circuits for \(g_n\) are over the same \(F\), and may use any constants from \(F\). The target is the existence of a polynomial-size circuit family for every factor family. It does not request a deterministic or randomized algorithm producing those circuits from circuits for \(f_n\), a common exponent valid for every field and family, or a complete factorization as an algorithmic output.

For a nonconstant irreducible polynomial \(u\), its multiplicity in a nonzero polynomial \(f\) is the largest integer \(e\ge0\) for which \(u^e\mid f\). The question includes every choice of a divisor, with any collection of such multiplicities permitted by \(f_n\). No square-free, separability or multiplicity-coprime-to-characteristic promise is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed universal implication or of its negation. A positive answer must establish a polynomial bound for circuits computing the actual factor family over the same base field, for every admissible family and every field of positive characteristic. A negative answer must establish a fixed positive-characteristic field and admissible families with \((f_n)\in\mathrm{VP}_{F}\), \(g_n\mid f_n\) for every \(n\), and
\[
\forall B,\ell\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge1,\quad L_F(g_n)>B(n+1)^{\ell}.
\]
No efficient method for generating a counterexample family is additionally required. A bound only for a positive-characteristic power of the factor, a circuit over an extension field without a proved return to the base field, or membership in a larger class does not settle the question. A proof of the failure of one factoring algorithm is not a refutation of this nonuniform closure statement.
cards.why: Factor closure asks whether multiplication can conceal a polynomial that is substantially harder to compute than the resulting product, even when all output degrees remain polynomially bounded. It is a structural question about the standard class of efficiently computable polynomial families. Its positive-characteristic form is also relevant to the scope of algebraic hardness-versus-randomness results, where extracting factors from circuit identities connects lower bounds with polynomial identity testing.

cards.title: Classical ideal-SVP hardness of ring-LWE in power-of-two cyclotomic rings
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge3\), do there exist constants \(C,K,a>0\), integers \(b\ge0,n_0\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized oracle algorithm that, for every power of two \(n\ge n_0\), reduces worst-case ideal-SVP in \(R_n=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^n+1)\) to the same-ring search-LWE problem defined below, with approximation factor
\[
\gamma(n,\alpha)=C\frac{\sqrt n}{\alpha}\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^b?
\]
The reduction must succeed with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input ideal basis, for every admissible oracle, and use at most \(K(L+m+t+1)^a\) classical bit operations and oracle calls on every run. Its queries must retain the degree \(n\), modulus \(q\), noise-family bound \(\alpha\) and sample count \(m\). The constants and algorithm may depend on \(c\), but not on the ideal or the other parameters.
cards.definitions:
Put \(K_n=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^n+1)\). Since \(n\) is a power of two, this is a number field with ring of integers \(R_n\). A nonzero integral ideal \(I\subseteq R_n\) is given by a full-rank integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\): its columns are the power-basis coefficient vectors of a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis of \(I\). The input is promised to generate a set closed under multiplication by \(X\), hence by every element of \(R_n\). All entries, dimensions and parameters are encoded explicitly in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is their total length.

Let \(\sigma_j\) be the embeddings sending \(X\) to the roots of \(X^n+1\). Use the canonical Euclidean norm
\[
\|v\|_{\rm can}^2=\sum_{j=1}^n|\sigma_j(v)|^2,
\qquad \lambda_1(I)=\min_{v\in I\setminus\{0\}}\|v\|_{\rm can}.
\]
The required output is a nonzero integer vector \(z\) such that the ideal element with coefficient vector \(Bz\) has norm at most \(\gamma(n,\alpha)\lambda_1(I)\). A short vector must actually be produced; deciding whether one exists is not the task. In this ring the canonical norm is \(\sqrt n\) times the coefficient Euclidean norm. Also, multiplying a shortest nonzero element by \(1,X,\ldots,X^{n-1}\) gives independent vectors of the same length, so the first and last successive minima of an ideal agree.

Admissible parameters have a prime \(q\le(n+2)^c\), integers \(1\le m\le(n+2)^c\), \(2\le t\le(n+2)^c\), and a rational \(\alpha=u/v\in(0,1/2]\), in lowest terms with \(u,v\le(n+2)^c\), satisfying \(\alpha q\ge(\log_2(n+2))^2\). Let \(R_{n,q}=R_n/qR_n\); its elements are encoded by \(n\) coefficients in \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\).

Here is the exact finite-output family of error distributions. Extend the power-basis coefficient space to \(K_{n,\mathbb R}=\mathbb R[X]/(X^n+1)\). Choose one embedding from each complex-conjugate pair and define the real isometry
\[
\tau(v)=\bigl(\sqrt2\operatorname{Re}\sigma_j(v),\sqrt2\operatorname{Im}\sigma_j(v)\bigr)_{j=1}^{n/2}\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
For any vector \(\rho=(\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_{n/2})\) with \(0<\rho_j\le\alpha\), sample independently two real Gaussian coordinates for pair \(j\), each of density \(\rho_j^{-1}\exp(-\pi x^2/\rho_j^2)\). Let \(e\in K_{n,\mathbb R}\) be their inverse image under \(\tau\). Expand \(nq e\) in the power basis, round each real coefficient to its nearest integer and reduce modulo \(q\). The resulting element of \(R_{n,q}\) has distribution \(\chi_\rho\). Ties occur with probability zero. The factor \(n\) is intentional: it converts rounding in the dual ring \(R_n^\vee=n^{-1}R_n\) to this ordinary-ring representation.

An admissible oracle \(A\) is a fixed randomized map from ordered lists of \(m\) pairs in \(R_{n,q}^2\) to \(R_{n,q}\cup\{\bot\}\). For every fixed \(\rho\) in the family, choose a uniformly random secret \(s\in R_{n,q}\), independently sample uniform \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in R_{n,q}\) and errors \(\eta_i\leftarrow\chi_\rho\), and form
\[
(a_i,a_i s+\eta_i)_{i=1}^m.
\]
On this input the oracle must output the sampled \(s\) with probability at least \(1/t\), averaged over the secret, samples and oracle randomness. The same oracle must satisfy this for every \(\rho\); neither the secret nor \(\rho\) is given as side information. It has fresh independent randomness on every invocation. Away from these distributional guarantees its answers are arbitrary. The reduction may make adaptive finite-list queries and must work for every such oracle.

Computation uses a classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine with fair independent random bits. Query construction, input reading, oracle-answer reading, all numerical approximations and output writing are charged; only the oracle's internal computation is excluded. Exact real Gaussians define probability distributions, not computational primitives available to the reduction. Its implementation must use finite arithmetic and include sampling errors in its total failure probability. There are no quantum operations, advice or additional oracles. This is a family-of-noises search target, not the stronger fixed spherical-noise or decision target.

cards.title: Capacity of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
cards.formal:
Determine the weighted capacity function
\[F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), \(P_{1},P_{2}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). The real memoryless channel is
\[Y_{1,t}=X_{1,t}+aX_{2,t}+Z_{1,t},\qquad Y_{2,t}=bX_{1,t}+X_{2,t}+Z_{2,t}.\]
The region \(C\) uses two independent private messages, deterministic separate encoders, average power over messages and time, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing joint average decoding error, as defined below. The required absolute accuracy is \(1/100\) bit per real channel use everywhere on this domain.
cards.definitions:
All five parameters are finite real numbers and remain fixed as block length grows. Negative, zero, and positive gains are included; powers may be zero or arbitrarily large. The two direct gains and the noise variances are normalized to one. For every \(i\in\{1,2\}\) and time \(t\), the noise \(Z_{i,t}\) has density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-z^{2}/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). All these noises are mutually independent and independent of both messages. There is no fading, channel state, or additional channel memory. Channel parameters and both codebooks are known to all terminals.

For a positive integer \(K\), let \([K]=\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\). An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code has \(n,K_{1},K_{2}\ge1\), two independent uniform messages \(M_{i}\in[K_{i}]\), deterministic encoders \(f_{i}:[K_{i}]\to\mathbb R^{n}\), and Borel-measurable decoders \(d_{i}:\mathbb R^{n}\to[K_{i}]\). Transmitter \(i\) sends \(X_{i}^{n}=f_{i}(M_{i})\), and receiver \(i\) estimates only its own message using \(d_{i}(Y_{i}^{n})\). Each code must satisfy
\[\frac{1}{nK_{i}}\sum_{m\in[K_{i}]}\sum_{t=1}^{n}f_{i}(m)_{t}^{2}\le P_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
This is a separate power budget for each transmitter, averaged over messages and time. It is not a bound on every symbol or every individual codeword, and power cannot be transferred between transmitters. The error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y_{1}^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Y_{2}^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
averaged over the independent uniform messages and all Gaussian noise. There is no maximal-error-over-messages requirement. The encoders may depend arbitrarily on time and their own messages, with arbitrary real codeword entries and no computation bound. They have no shared random seed, common message, feedback, or communication link; neither encoder knows the other message. The receivers cannot communicate. Predetermined time sharing, unequal powers in different phases, and arbitrary temporal dependence within each codeword are allowed subject to the displayed average budgets. There is no secrecy or prescribed signaling-distribution constraint.

All rate logarithms have base two. A nonnegative rate pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\) is achievable if there is a code for each integer block length \(n\ge1\), with message sizes \(K_{i,n}\), such that \(P_{e,n}\to0\) and
\[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_{2}K_{i,n}}{n}\ge R_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
The region \(C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})\) is the Euclidean closure of all achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\), where \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\); hence \(F\) is finite. These are bits per one real scalar channel use, not per complex channel use. No finite block code must attain a boundary rate. The weights include both endpoints, and the exact supporting function determines the closed region. The task has real mathematical parameters; it does not silently restrict them or the codebooks to rational encodings.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on \(\mathbb R^{2}\times\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\times[0,1]\) and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that, for every tuple in this domain,
\[|g(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)-F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must justify both sides of this error against the operational code definition, using its average-power and average-error conventions and bits per real use. Certified lower and upper bounds of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by their midpoint. An exact function also qualifies. A formula or another unambiguous mathematical description may be used; no single-letter syntax, fixed number of auxiliary variables, polynomial evaluation bound, or finite encoding of arbitrary real inputs is required. Any proposed evaluation rule must have a proved meaning and the stated guarantee on the full real domain. An unevaluated restatement of the capacity optimization or its limiting code definition, a sampled plot, and bounds with an unclosed gap do not determine the answer. Sum capacity alone, a restricted signaling optimum, a special interference regime, or an asymptotic high-power approximation is insufficient. The fixed tolerance does not assert an exact capacity theorem.

cards.context:
Two separately informed transmitters use the same medium, so each receiver observes its desired signal plus interference and Gaussian noise. The point-to-point rate \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\) is an individual upper bound, but the two upper bounds generally cannot be reached together. The target describes every tradeoff between the independent conversations; knowing only their best total rate leaves other supporting weights undetermined.

The general two-user model is a foundational network information theory problem. Han–Kobayashi regions are established achievable inner bounds, and several structured parameter regimes have exact capacity or exact sum-capacity results. Shang and Chen’s monograph explicitly distinguishes these two kinds of conclusions. An optimal value within one specified signaling family is also different from a converse bounding every permitted code.

For strong interference, \(|a|\ge1\) and \(|b|\ge1\), the known capacity region is given by \(0\le R_{i}\le c_{i}\) and
\[R_{1}+R_{2}\le\min\!\left\{\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{1}+a^{2}P_{2}),\ \tfrac12\log_{2}(1+b^{2}P_{1}+P_{2})\right\}.\]
These are the two Gaussian multiple-access sum bounds in this card’s real normalization. With \(a=b=0\), capacity is the rectangle \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\). The solved cases explain why an answer must retain both gains and both powers, rather than assume symmetry or a single interference-strength ordering.

Etkin, Tse and Wang establish the celebrated universal one-bit approximation using achievable and outer regions. The checked preprint’s formal model is complex-valued, and its error notion is an additive coordinate gap, not a bound on the error of a plotted sum-rate curve. That constant-gap theorem is a major approximate characterization, but it is not a certificate at this card’s much smaller tolerance in bits per real use. Its units and power convention must be accounted for in any precise transfer to this model.

Nair and Ng prove that allowing temporally correlated vector Gaussian inputs in the multiletter Han–Kobayashi region gives the same region as scalar Gaussian inputs when the comparison includes time sharing and its power allocation. This is an invariance theorem within a signaling class. It does not rule out other input distributions or establish full capacity. Huleihel and Merhav’s older preprint claiming an improvement from Gaussian memory was withdrawn in April 2018; its original abstract must not be counted as a valid advance.

Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 work settles a structural conjecture about the Gaussian-signaling region for the one-sided, or Z, channel. Under its explicit parameter condition, multiplexing is unnecessary for the optimum of that inner region. The theorem does not assert that the inner region equals capacity for all Z channels.

Their January 2026 manuscript gives parameters where non-Gaussian distributions outperform Gaussian ones in a restricted single-phase superposition region without power control. Its Conjecture 1 still concerns the full Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region including power allocation over time. Section II.D explains that the new counterexample regime is disjoint from the regime in which the previous no-multiplexing theorem applies. Thus these results do not jointly yield a counterexample to the full capacity conjecture. Remark 2 also records the authors’ inability to verify parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim.

Gohari, Nair and Zhao’s February 2026 manuscript combines converse bounds through auxiliary receivers. The full Gaussian discussion in Section II.C restricts its matching corner, sum-rate and slope conclusions to the stated very-weak-interference regime and corresponding one-sided specializations. These conclusions must not be expanded to arbitrary weak interference merely from the broader abstract wording. The paper supplies an outer bound, not the general capacity function.

Khandani’s current v12, posted on 7 September 2026, claims that Gaussian Han–Kobayashi signaling attains weak-interference capacity with at most two time-sharing phases. Its equations use nonnegative squared cross-gain parameters under square roots; those symbols are not this card’s possibly signed amplitude gains. Sections 7–8 present the claimed converse and optimality conclusion. This review checked that statement and scope but did not establish the correctness of the full proof for unrestricted codes. Nair–Zhao’s January criticism predates this revision and is not automatically a refutation of it. The claim covers a major subdomain and is recorded under uncertain status, without asserting a solution over all real gains.

The formulation uses this real-parameter supporting-function target on 12 September 2026. The present review retains its full domain, average-power convention, and absolute \(1/100\) numerical acceptance. It does not add a requirement for a particular finite-letter characterization, and it does not infer fixed-tolerance unsolvability from sources discussing exact capacity.

cards.title: Decidability of unconditional entropy inequalities
cards.formal:
Does one deterministic Turing algorithm exist that always halts and decides the following problem? Its input is an integer \(n\ge1\) and rational coefficients \(a_S\) for the nonempty subsets \(S\subseteq[n]\). It must answer YES exactly when
\[
 \sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n]}a_S H(X_S)\ge0
\]
holds for every joint distribution of \(n\) finite-valued discrete random variables. The finite alphabet sizes are unrestricted, and the inequality has no premises or affine constant.
cards.definitions:
Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input gives \(n\) in binary and a finite list of pairs \((S,a_S)\) with distinct nonempty subsets of \([n]\). A subset is encoded as an increasing list of its binary indices, and a coefficient as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Missing subsets have coefficient zero. Zero coefficients and an empty coefficient list are allowed. All delimiters and list lengths are explicitly encoded; malformed inputs may be rejected. This is a finite rational input, with no real-number oracle or distribution description.

For the semantic validity test, independently quantify over every choice of positive integers \(r_1,\ldots,r_n\) and every joint probability mass function
\[
 p:\prod_{i=1}^n\{1,\ldots,r_i\}\longrightarrow[0,1],
 \qquad \sum_x p(x)=1.
\]
The probability values may be arbitrary real numbers. Let \(X_i\) be coordinate \(i\) of a tuple sampled from \(p\). For a nonempty \(S\subseteq[n]\), \(X_S\) is the tuple of coordinates with indices in \(S\), in increasing order. Its marginal mass function \(p_S\) is obtained by summing over the other coordinates. Define Shannon entropy in bits by
\[
 H(X_S)=-\sum_z p_S(z)\log_2 p_S(z),\qquad 0\log_2 0=0.
\]
All these sums are finite. An alphabet size may be one, and zero-probability outcomes are allowed. The integers \(r_i\) are quantified over, not bounded by the input or supplied to the deciding algorithm.

Validity means the displayed non-strict inequality holds for every such distribution. Invalidity means that at least one finite-alphabet distribution gives a strictly negative value. No numerical separation from zero is promised. In particular, valid inequalities can achieve equality, and a total decider must handle those boundary cases.

There are no assumptions of independence, conditional independence, functional dependence, prescribed marginals, bounded support or bounded alphabet size. Coefficients of either sign are allowed. The input expresses one homogeneous linear inequality with right-hand side zero. It does not express an implication with entropy constraints as premises, a Boolean combination of inequalities, a nonzero affine term or a nonlinear function of entropies.

The term entropy inequality here includes all universal linear inequalities in Shannon entropies. It is not restricted to the class often called Shannon-type inequalities, meaning those deducible by nonnegative combinations of the elementary conditional-entropy and conditional-mutual-information inequalities. Deciding membership in that narrower class is a different problem.

A decision algorithm is a single finite deterministic Turing program returning the correct YES or NO answer after finitely many steps on every valid finite encoding, for every input value of \(n\). No polynomial or other prescribed running-time or space bound is requested. Separate procedures for only finitely many values of \(n\), a semidecision procedure that may fail to halt, or an oracle for a noncomputable real quantity do not meet this definition.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction of a total decision algorithm and a proof of its termination and exact semantic correctness for every input; or give a complete Lean-checked proof that the set of valid input inequalities is undecidable.

A new valid inequality, a counterexample to one candidate inequality, or an incomplete proof-generation procedure answers only individual instances. A procedure requiring a promised numerical gap, a fixed alphabet bound or a fixed number of variables is insufficient unless a proved effective reduction covers the full unrestricted problem. Undecidability for conditional inequalities or a richer input language does not settle this question without a valid reduction to this exact homogeneous unconditional form. There is no numerical approximation tolerance on the validity decision.

cards.context:
Elementary Shannon inequalities supply a useful finite proof method at each number of variables, but do not characterize all valid entropy inequalities. Failure to obtain an elementary derivation is therefore not a proof of invalidity.

Unconditional validity is known to be co-recursively enumerable. That upper classification does not supply a procedure that halts on every valid input, which is essential to this target.

Undecidability has been proved for conditional information inequalities and conditional-independence implication. Those problems permit exact premises, and deleting them changes the mathematical statement.

The source obtains complexity classifications after changing the semantic domain or imposing syntactic restrictions. These results do not decide arbitrary inequalities over all finite-valued entropy vectors.

Recent work derives infinite collections of additional inequalities and investigates generation methods. The 2026 five-variable enumeration concerns one such method; no completeness theorem for all unconditional inequalities is supplied.

cards.title: Rate–distortion tradeoff for distributed lossy source coding
cards.formal: Determine \[F_{\mathrm{RD}}(P,d_1,d_2,D_1,D_2,\lambda)=\inf_{(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal R(P,d_1,d_2,D_1,D_2)}\bigl(\lambda R_1+(1-\lambda)R_2\bigr)\] for every finite-alphabet memoryless source pair, finite distortion tables, feasible distortion targets and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), where \(\mathcal R\) is the rate region for separate encoders and a joint decoder.
cards.definitions: The source alphabets \(\mathcal X_i\) and reproduction alphabets \(\widehat{\mathcal X}_i\), for \(i=1,2\), are nonempty finite sets. The pairs \((X_{1,t},X_{2,t})\) are independent identically distributed draws from an arbitrary real probability table \(P\) on \(\mathcal X_1\times\mathcal X_2\). Distortions are finite-valued functions \(d_i:\mathcal X_i\times\widehat{\mathcal X}_i\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). Write \(P_i\) for the marginal source law and \(D_{i,\min}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X_i}P_i(x)\min_{z\in\widehat{\mathcal X}_i}d_i(x,z)\). The domain requires finite real \(D_i\ge D_{i,\min}\). An \(n\)-block code consists of deterministic encoders \(f_{i,n}:\mathcal X_i^n\to[M_{i,n}]\), where \([M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}\) and \(M_{i,n}\ge1\), and a deterministic decoder from the pair of indices to \(\widehat{\mathcal X}_1^n\times\widehat{\mathcal X}_2^n\). Each encoder sees only its own source block. For the resulting reproductions define \(\Delta_{i,n}=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[d_i(X_{i,t},\widehat X_{i,t})]\). A nonnegative pair is achievable if, along some \(n_j\to\infty\), codes satisfy \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2M_{i,n_j}\le R_i\) and \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}\Delta_{i,n_j}\le D_i\) for both sources. The region \(\mathcal R\) is the closure of achievable pairs. There is no interaction, extra side information, computational restriction or variable-length encoding; distortion is expected per-symbol distortion. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. Transmitting both source blocks and selecting minimum-distortion reproductions establishes feasibility on the stated domain; smaller distortion targets, which would give an empty region, are excluded. The region is convex and upward closed. Its nonnegative lower supporting values describe its lower rate boundary. The target is finite and nonnegative, in weighted bits per source pair. All tables are mathematical real objects, with no algorithmic representation requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the whole source, distortion and weight domain above and a Lean proof of \(|g-F_{\mathrm{RD}}|\le1/100\) pointwise. This is an error bound on the weighted rate in bits per source pair; the distortion constraints remain exact. Prove both sides of the bound, or determine the function exactly. A finite sample of values or a restatement of the operational infimum or limit is insufficient. No specified formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed.
